segments.text: How to practice guitar and train your creativity by Sam Russell. Introduction.
This book is about creativity, what it is, what it is not, and what you can do to become more creative.
We'll also look at how to practice the guitar effectively. After all, what's the point in being creative if you can't put that into practice on your guitar?
How to learn effectively and a few practical points on guitar and guitar equipment.
Creativity and how to practice effectively is a widely misunderstood subject.
People will write themselves off as not being creative before they have given themselves a chance
and give up on playing the guitar because they don't understand how to practice effectively
and as such do not make any progress.
I hope that by writing this book you will be encouraged to try out some of the ideas
and either become creative or enhance the creativity that you already have.

chapters.title: Section 1. An overview of creativity

segments.text: is and how you can go about being more creative. Section 1. An overview of creativity.
What creativity is not. While I don't want to be too negative, it's important to clear up some
misconceptions as quickly as possible by having a quick conversation about what creativity is not.
Creativity doesn't come out of nowhere. Creativity isn't genetic. People aren't born with a creativity
gene or a guitar-playing gene. You aren't too old to be creative. There is no such thing as talent
or natural ability. There is only practice. This has been proven, footnote 1 and 2.
Anyone who chooses to read a book about creativity, or read in general, is intelligent
enough to be creative. What is creativity? So what is creativity? Oxford languages define it as
the use of imagination or original ideas to create something, inventiveness.
Footnote 3. According to Wikipedia, creativity is,
Creativity is a phenomenon whereby something new and valuable is formed.
Footnote 4. And finally, the Cambridge Dictionary defines creativity as,
The ability to produce or use original and unusual ideas. Footnote 5. From looking at
these definitions, we can see that creativity involves the creation of new ideas. When we think
about new ideas, there are two types. Original ideas. Synthetic ideas. Original ideas are truly
new ideas. They are generations ahead of their time. When we think of creativity, people often
tend to think about this. For example, inventing the light bulb or discovering calculus. Synthetic
ideas are ideas that combine previous ideas to create something new. For example, take something
you already eat, such as roast beef, and put it in a sandwich to create a roast beef sandwich.
The majority of new ideas are synthetic ideas. You can think of this as standing on the shoulders
of giants. This gives us a clue as to what is involved in creativity. If we are going to combine
ideas that others have created, we need to understand them. This is why learning and
studying is a fundamental pillar of creativity, one that is often overlooked. After all, when we
think of creativity, we rarely think about someone sitting down and studying. When it comes to
discussing creativity, often we find the discussion ends here, if it gets this far at all. But there
is another step that we need to take. Now we know that creativity involves working with ideas,
and creating new ideas, a question we should ask is, how do we go about creating new ideas?
New ideas are the same thing as problem-solving. Fundamentally, creativity boils down to problem
solving. Creativity comes about from asking a question and seeking the answer. The question
could be a simple one, such as, what notes should I play over a C chord? Or it could be more complex,
such as, can I compose a sonata with a main theme in the key of a minor with the time signature 7-8
that modulates to a secondary theme in the key of a flat minor with the time signature 11-16?
When we have a question such as the one I asked above with the sonata,
we give ourselves a framework from which we can get our creative juices flowing and start working on creating.
What we are going to do with this book is break down in detail how this process works and what we can do to become more creative.
We'll look at the errors that people commonly make when approaching creativity and practical steps that you can take to become more creative.
The Creativity Path
We can think of developing our creative abilities as a path which has three main steps.
Studying concepts
Guided problem solving
Self-directed problem solving
Let's briefly talk about each step.
Step 1. Studying concepts
Studying concepts is fundamental to becoming creative.
You cannot create new ideas without understanding the ideas that already exist.
We also want to avoid reinventing the wheel.
By studying techniques, ideas and best practices that already exist,
we can get up to speed with our contemporaries and start working on something new. Before becoming
a musician and composer, I studied astrophysics at university, eventually gaining a master's in
physics with astrophysics. Up until my graduation, I thought of learning as regurgitating facts.
I thought that the point of studying was to memorize various facts. I'm not sure if this
is more damning of myself or the education system, probably a bit of both, but that's what I thought
it was. However, this is not what learning is about. Learning is about understanding concepts,
the context that particular concepts apply to, and the essentials that define different concepts.
We are going to cover learning in quite some detail, from the epistemology behind concepts
to practical ways you can improve your learning and what you should be learning.
Step 2. Guided Problem Solving
The next step to being creative is guided problem solving.
If you have a teacher that is any good, after teaching you something they will get you to work on it.
If they are teaching you how to find the notes in a major chord,
they will then give you a set of notes and ask what major chords they build,
or give you a major chord and ask what notes it is made of.
Having the theory from studying the concepts is one thing,
it is another to apply that to problem-solving. The vital component here is that the problem-solving
is guided. It is appropriate and directly applicable to what you have just been studying.
This idea has been understood for centuries by authors who write textbooks and leave a list of
questions at the end of each chapter. Those questions are guided problem-solving. You can
even take this concept and apply it to boxing. When a coach is looking for the first match for
a new fighter, they don't go and put their rookie fighter up against the world heavyweight champion.
They find someone suitable at their level. Step 3. Self-directed problem solving. This is the final
step and often the most missed out step. Once you have gone through steps 1 and 2, you want to start
setting your own problems to solve or find ways to apply your new knowledge to problems that are
different to the ones that your instructor or book has set. This is where creativity comes into play.
To return to the example of major chords, after your instructor has covered the theory behind how
a major chord works, you could then see how many different ways you could play them on guitar.
How many ways can you play them holding down all the notes in the chord at one time?
How many ways can you play a major chord playing each note one after the other?
How many ways can you play a major chord by using tapping?
You can quickly see that we can take the concept of a major chord
and explode it into an enormous set of possibilities and problems to solve.
As you become more advanced in your understanding,
you will find that the possibilities open to you become greater,
which is why we have such a diverse amount of music today.
The Spiral Theory of Knowledge
Something worth mentioning before we move on
is the spiral theory of knowledge. I first heard this formalized in a book called
Understanding Objectivism, footnote 6, which is an edited transcription of a series of lectures
that were built around psychoepistemology, which is the study of how we approach thinking.
Often when thinking about the pursuit of knowledge, we think about it linearly,
as a line from A to Z. We start at A, then learn the different elements of our subject until we
reach Z, at which point we know the subject. This is a linear theory of knowledge.
Figure 1, linear theory of knowledge. Instead, we want to think of the pursuit of knowledge like
this. We start at a dot from which emanates several lines, which are the topics within our
subject. We move in a spiral out from the center, cutting through each line progressively further
along that line. Each time we hit another line, we are repeating steps one to three.
In this manner, it is easy to understand that learning is a process and not an event. We don't
finish learning music. We don't finish learning guitar, and we simply move to the next point on
our spiral, looking at more complex applications of ideas that we previously studied. Figure two,
Spiral Theory of Knowledge
Other factors
That impact our creative potential
The creative path and the spiral theory of knowledge
form the fundamentals of becoming creative.
But many other factors can impact our creative potential,
which includes our
Environment
Approach to studying
Mindset
Health
Time management
And we are going to explore each of those,
how they impact your creativity
and how you can use them to optimize your creativity. Mindset fundamentals. What is mindset?
Mindset is how we think about something. When it comes to creativity, we must approach it the right
way. Approaching creativity the wrong way leads to extreme frustration, which more often than not
leads to giving up entirely and regurgitating the mantra of, maybe I'm just not creative.
There are some basic approaches or best practices that I have developed over the years from reflecting on my behavior and also from helping my students with problems that they face.
The myth of talent.
The difference between being talented and natural talent.
There are two ways of looking at talent as a reflection of skill or as a divine genetic gift.
Talent as a reflection of skill.
You might say that a talented person is someone who has achieved a very high level of skill.
This could be a guitar player, a songwriter, an artist, an architect, or a salesperson.
This could apply to any human skill.
The key idea here is that the talents in question have been achieved through deliberate practice by the individual in question.
Talent as a divine genetic lottery
The second way of looking at talent is the idea of natural talent.
This is the idea that talent comes from someplace that is external to you, that you have no control over.
This could be divine or genetic, two variables over which you have no control.
Natural talent is the idea that someone has an innate ability, that is genetic ability, with a skill.
Natural talent is the idea that someone popped out of the womb with the ability to play guitar great from day one.
Hopefully, you're already starting to see the idea doesn't make any sense.
Natural talent is a myth.
There is no such thing as a gene that makes you great at playing the guitar.
Natural talent myths.
1. Apples and oranges comparison.
The first myth about talent we'll look at is a logical fallacy.
the apples and oranges comparison. We can go to a show and watch someone like Steve Vai on stage
play incredible music without missing a note. Everything he does looks flawless. It looks so
easy. Everything he does seems to flow naturally. But when we try to do it, when we learn, it's
different. We struggle. It doesn't come naturally to us. Sometimes we conclude that the person we
are comparing ourselves to is naturally talented, and we are not. The reasoning goes like this.
It looks natural for Steve Vai to play, but it is not natural for me to learn,
therefore Steve Vai must be naturally talented, and I am not. However, this is a logical fallacy.
When we make this type of comparison, we are comparing two things that cannot be compared,
our learning of guitar to another person's performance after they spent time learning.
We are comparing the rate at which we learn to the results of the time they spent learning.
These are two different things. It is illogical to compare them. It doesn't make any sense to
compare your ability at the start of learning something to the ability of someone who has
been practicing in that field for years. Just like you wouldn't compare the price of a...

Coca-Cola to the price of a gold watch and say, this gold watch is expensive compared to a can of cola, therefore it is a bad deal. We can't compare how we learn to how someone else performs. So what should we compare our playing against? Compare your playing today to your playing last week and strive to improve it just a tiny bit, just a little.
If you strive to improve week by week and commit to learning for several years,
you will not believe the levels of playing you can reach.
If you just keep going, improving week by week,
you will be able to reach any level of playing that you could dream of.
Natural Talent Myths
2. Our experience is unique.

paragraphs.ca: Per tornar a l'exemple dels acords majors, després que el teu instructor hagi tractat la teoria de com funciona un acord major, podries veure de quantes maneres diferents els pots tocar a la guitarra.

paragraphs.en: How many ways can you play them holding down all the notes in the chord at one time? How many ways can you play a major chord playing each note one after the other?
paragraphs.ca: De quantes maneres els pots tocar prement totes les notes de l'acord alhora? De quantes maneres pots tocar un acord major tocant cada nota una darrere l'altra?

paragraphs.en: How many ways can you play a major chord by using tapping? You can quickly see that we can take the concept of a major chord and explode it into an enormous set of possibilities and problems to solve.
paragraphs.ca: De quantes maneres pots tocar un acord major fent servir el tapping? De seguida veus que podem agafar el concepte d'acord major i fer-lo esclatar en un conjunt enorme de possibilitats i de problemes per resoldre.

paragraphs.en: As you become more advanced in your understanding, you will find that the possibilities open to you become greater, which is why we have such a diverse amount of music today.
paragraphs.ca: A mesura que avancis en la teva comprensió, trobaràs que les possibilitats que se t'obren són més grans, i per això avui tenim una música tan diversa.

paragraphs.en: The Spiral Theory of Knowledge Something worth mentioning before we move on is the spiral theory of knowledge. I first heard this formalized in a book called
paragraphs.ca: La teoria espiral del coneixement Una cosa que val la pena esmentar abans de continuar és la teoria espiral del coneixement. La primera vegada que la vaig sentir formulada va ser en un llibre titulat

paragraphs.en: Understanding Objectivism, footnote 6, which is an edited transcription of a series of lectures that were built around psychoepistemology, which is the study of how we approach thinking.
paragraphs.ca: Understanding Objectivism, nota 6, que és una transcripció editada d'una sèrie de conferències construïdes al voltant de la psicoepistemologia, que és l'estudi de com abordem el pensament.

paragraphs.en: Often when thinking about the pursuit of knowledge, we think about it linearly, as a line from A to Z. We start at A, then learn the different elements of our subject until we reach Z, at which point we know the subject. This is a linear theory of knowledge.
paragraphs.ca: Sovint, quan pensem en la recerca del coneixement, la pensem de manera lineal, com una línia de la A a la Z. Comencem per la A i anem aprenent els diferents elements de la nostra matèria fins que arribem a la Z, moment en què ja coneixem la matèria. Aquesta és una teoria lineal del coneixement.

paragraphs.en: Figure 1, linear theory of knowledge. Instead, we want to think of the pursuit of knowledge like this. We start at a dot from which emanates several lines, which are the topics within our subject. We move in a spiral out from the center, cutting through each line progressively further along that line. Each time we hit another line, we are repeating steps one to three.
paragraphs.ca: Figura 1, teoria lineal del coneixement. En canvi, volem pensar en la recerca del coneixement així. Comencem en un punt del qual emanen diverses línies, que són els temes dins de la nostra matèria. Ens movem en espiral cap enfora des del centre, travessant cada línia progressivament més enllà en aquella línia. Cada vegada que topem amb una altra línia, repetim els passos u a tres.

paragraphs.en: In this manner, it is easy to understand that learning is a process and not an event. We don't finish learning music. We don't finish learning guitar, and we simply move to the next point on our spiral, looking at more complex applications of ideas that we previously studied. Figure two, Spiral Theory of Knowledge Other factors That impact our creative potential The creative path and the spiral theory of knowledge form the fundamentals of becoming creative.
paragraphs.ca: D'aquesta manera, és fàcil entendre que aprendre és un procés i no un esdeveniment. No acabem d'aprendre música. No acabem d'aprendre guitarra, sinó que simplement passem al punt següent de la nostra espiral, mirant aplicacions més complexes d'idees que havíem estudiat abans. Figura dos, teoria espiral del coneixement Altres factors que incideixen en el nostre potencial creatiu El camí de la creativitat i la teoria espiral del coneixement formen els fonaments per esdevenir creatiu.

paragraphs.en: But many other factors can impact our creative potential, which includes our Environment Approach to studying Mindset Health Time management And we are going to explore each of those, how they impact your creativity and how you can use them to optimize your creativity. Mindset fundamentals. What is mindset?
paragraphs.ca: Però molts altres factors poden afectar el nostre potencial creatiu, com ara el nostre entorn, l'enfocament de l'estudi, la mentalitat, la salut i la gestió del temps. I explorarem cadascun d'aquests factors, com afecten la teva creativitat i com els pots fer servir per optimitzar-la. Fonaments de la mentalitat. Què és la mentalitat?

paragraphs.en: Mindset is how we think about something. When it comes to creativity, we must approach it the right way. Approaching creativity the wrong way leads to extreme frustration, which more often than not leads to giving up entirely and regurgitating the mantra of, maybe I'm just not creative.
paragraphs.ca: La mentalitat és com pensem sobre una cosa. Pel que fa a la creativitat, ens hi hem d'acostar de la manera correcta. Acostar-se a la creativitat de la manera equivocada porta a una frustració extrema, que molt sovint porta a rendir-se del tot i a repetir el mantra de «potser simplement no soc creatiu».

paragraphs.en: There are some basic approaches or best practices that I have developed over the years from reflecting on my behavior and also from helping my students with problems that they face.
paragraphs.ca: Hi ha alguns enfocaments bàsics o bones pràctiques que he desenvolupat al llarg dels anys reflexionant sobre el meu comportament i també ajudant els meus alumnes amb els problemes que afronten.

paragraphs.en: The myth of talent.
paragraphs.ca: El mite del talent.

paragraphs.en: The difference between being talented and natural talent. There are two ways of looking at talent as a reflection of skill or as a divine genetic gift.
paragraphs.ca: La diferència entre ser talentós i el talent natural. Hi ha dues maneres d'entendre el talent: com a reflex de l'habilitat o com a do genètic diví.

paragraphs.en: Talent as a reflection of skill. You might say that a talented person is someone who has achieved a very high level of skill.
paragraphs.ca: El talent com a reflex de l'habilitat. Podríem dir que una persona talentosa és algú que ha assolit un nivell d'habilitat molt alt.

paragraphs.en: This could be a guitar player, a songwriter, an artist, an architect, or a salesperson. This could apply to any human skill.
paragraphs.ca: Podria ser un guitarrista, un compositor de cançons, un artista, un arquitecte o un venedor. Això es podria aplicar a qualsevol habilitat humana.

paragraphs.en: The key idea here is that the talents in question have been achieved through deliberate practice by the individual in question.
paragraphs.ca: La idea clau aquí és que els talents en qüestió s'han assolit mitjançant la pràctica deliberada per part de la persona en qüestió.

paragraphs.en: Talent as a divine genetic lottery The second way of looking at talent is the idea of natural talent. This is the idea that talent comes from someplace that is external to you, that you have no control over.
paragraphs.ca: El talent com a loteria genètica divina La segona manera d'entendre el talent és la idea del talent natural. És la idea que el talent ve d'algun lloc extern a tu, sobre el qual no tens cap control.

paragraphs.en: This could be divine or genetic, two variables over which you have no control. Natural talent is the idea that someone has an innate ability, that is genetic ability, with a skill.
paragraphs.ca: Podria ser diví o genètic, dues variables sobre les quals no tens cap control. El talent natural és la idea que algú té una capacitat innata, és a dir genètica, per a una habilitat.

paragraphs.en: Natural talent is the idea that someone popped out of the womb with the ability to play guitar great from day one. Hopefully, you're already starting to see the idea doesn't make any sense.
paragraphs.ca: El talent natural és la idea que algú va sortir del ventre de la mare amb la capacitat de tocar la guitarra genial des del primer dia. Espero que ja comencis a veure que la idea no té cap sentit.

paragraphs.en: Natural talent is a myth. There is no such thing as a gene that makes you great at playing the guitar.
paragraphs.ca: El talent natural és un mite. No existeix cap gen que et faci ser genial tocant la guitarra.

paragraphs.en: Natural talent myths.
paragraphs.ca: Mites del talent natural.

paragraphs.en: 1. Apples and oranges comparison.
paragraphs.ca: 1. La comparació de pomes i taronges.

paragraphs.en: The first myth about talent we'll look at is a logical fallacy. the apples and oranges comparison. We can go to a show and watch someone like Steve Vai on stage play incredible music without missing a note. Everything he does looks flawless. It looks so easy. Everything he does seems to flow naturally. But when we try to do it, when we learn, it's different. We struggle. It doesn't come naturally to us. Sometimes we conclude that the person we
paragraphs.ca: El primer mite sobre el talent que veurem és una fal·làcia lògica: la comparació de pomes i taronges. Podem anar a un concert i veure algú com Steve Vai sobre l'escenari tocant música increïble sense fallar cap nota. Tot el que fa sembla impecable. Sembla tan fàcil. Tot el que fa sembla fluir amb naturalitat. Però quan ho intentem fer nosaltres, quan aprenem, és diferent. Ens costa. No ens surt natural. De vegades concloem que la persona amb qui

paragraphs.en: are comparing ourselves to is naturally talented, and we are not. The reasoning goes like this. It looks natural for Steve Vai to play, but it is not natural for me to learn, therefore Steve Vai must be naturally talented, and I am not. However, this is a logical fallacy.
paragraphs.ca: ens comparem té talent natural, i nosaltres no. El raonament és així: sembla natural que en Steve Vai toqui, però no és natural que jo aprengui, per tant en Steve Vai deu tenir talent natural i jo no. Tanmateix, això és una fal·làcia lògica.

paragraphs.en: When we make this type of comparison, we are comparing two things that cannot be compared, our learning of guitar to another person's performance after they spent time learning.
paragraphs.ca: Quan fem aquest tipus de comparació, comparem dues coses que no es poden comparar: el nostre aprenentatge de la guitarra amb l'actuació d'una altra persona després que hagi passat temps aprenent.

paragraphs.en: We are comparing the rate at which we learn to the results of the time they spent learning. These are two different things. It is illogical to compare them. It doesn't make any sense to compare your ability at the start of learning something to the ability of someone who has been practicing in that field for years. Just like you wouldn't compare the price of a...
paragraphs.ca: Comparem la velocitat a què aprenem amb els resultats del temps que l'altra persona ha passat aprenent. Són dues coses diferents. És il·lògic comparar-les. No té cap sentit comparar la teva habilitat a l'inici d'aprendre una cosa amb l'habilitat d'algú que ha estat practicant en aquell camp durant anys. Igual que no compararies el preu d'una...

paragraphs.en: Coca-Cola to the price of a gold watch and say, this gold watch is expensive compared to a can of cola, therefore it is a bad deal. We can't compare how we learn to how someone else performs. So what should we compare our playing against? Compare your playing today to your playing last week and strive to improve it just a tiny bit, just a little.
paragraphs.ca: Coca-Cola amb el preu d'un rellotge d'or i diries: aquest rellotge d'or és car comparat amb una llauna de cola, per tant és una mala compra. No podem comparar com aprenem nosaltres amb com rendeix una altra persona. I doncs, amb què hauríem de comparar la nostra manera de tocar? Compara com toques avui amb com tocaves la setmana passada i esforça't per millorar-ho només una miqueta, només una mica.

paragraphs.en: If you strive to improve week by week and commit to learning for several years, you will not believe the levels of playing you can reach.
paragraphs.ca: Si t'esforces per millorar setmana rere setmana i et compromets a aprendre durant uns quants anys, no et creuràs els nivells de tocada que pots arribar a assolir.

paragraphs.en: If you just keep going, improving week by week, you will be able to reach any level of playing that you could dream of.
paragraphs.ca: Si simplement continues, millorant setmana rere setmana, podràs assolir qualsevol nivell de tocada que puguis somiar.

paragraphs.en: Natural Talent Myths
paragraphs.ca: Mites del talent natural

chapters.title_ca: Secció 1. Una visió general de la creativitat

segments.text: 2. Our experience is unique.
Oh, but it's different for me.
Yeah? How do you know?
We are all individuals
We have our thoughts, values and ambitions
But we are also all human
We have a lot in common
We all need to eat a similar amount
Drink a similar amount
And maintain a certain core body temperature
So the question is
Is learning something that is a similar experience for most people?
Do some people learn faster than others?
Or to get to the point
The question we often ask ourselves is
Why do I learn so slowly compared to everyone else?
I'm going to say that for most of the population, we learn at a pretty similar rate.
However, some factors differ between people which affect the rate of progress,
how well we focus on a task, the questions we ask ourselves while we are learning,
the amount of time we put into a task, the mindset that we have in approaching a task,
our environment when learning.
Do you think Steve Vai picks four notes, then neurotically worries that he did it wrong
and spends three hours googling the right way to do it?
Or do you think he just gets on with it?
While I can't say for sure, I'm guessing it's the latter.
Did Ingui Malmsteen play the guitar for ten minutes a day?
Or did he practice relentlessly, skipping school and falling asleep with his guitar?
These areas are all areas that we can actively improve
to learn guitar faster and reach higher levels of playing. When it comes down to it, we all learn at
pretty much the same rate. By improving the above areas, we accelerate our rate of progress.
I get what you're saying, but what if I do learn slowly? There is one response and two solutions
to this problem. The first is you have to look at this like a mathematical equation.
If you learn slowly, then you can still achieve high levels of playing by putting in more practice time, which is high-quality practice.
Therefore, plan out ways to increase your practice time on guitar, and you can still achieve high levels of playing.
So what if you learn slowly? It doesn't matter.
The second way is to find a great teacher to help you.
You might have to sift through a few different teachers to find one that works well for you.
Having someone give you advice and feedback, answer your questions,
and help make sure that you correctly understand and practice various topics
and have a plan for doing so, is a great way to accelerate your progress on the guitar.
But the truth of the matter is, you don't learn slowly.
Every second you spend considering that thought is one you could have spent practicing and improving.
Ironically, worrying that you are a slow learner will slow down your learning.
Next time you catch yourself worrying about whether or not you are a slow learner,
pinch yourself, literally, and just get back to practicing the guitar.
Talent myth 3. Expert amnesia
Sometimes talented people themselves spread the myth of talent.
Have you ever watched instructional DVDs of great guitar players?
I know I have. Sometimes these DVDs really suck.
Let me clarify.
These DVDs have awesome licks and great ideas to work on,
but they rarely explain how to play those awesome ideas.
When some guitar players are asked how to play XYZ lick,
they say, just do it.
When they are asked how they learned, they say they just did it.
And boom, the myth of natural talent has new life.
However, this is not quite true.
This is an effect referred to as expert amnesia.
This is when someone has reached an incredibly high level of ability and cannot remember what
it is like to be at a lower level. This is why sometimes high-level guitar players struggle to
effectively teach beginner guitar players because it is incredibly difficult for them to understand
things from the beginner's perspective. You may have experienced this yourself when taking lessons.
A teacher may give you something and tell you to play it, you struggle, and then they get frustrated
with you. I have one student who had a previous teacher tell her that she probably wouldn't be
able to play the guitar. She now writes her own music, can freely improvise across a variety of
scales, and is studying counterpoint. The problem wasn't her natural ability to play the guitar,
it was that things were not sufficiently explained to her. The effect of expert amnesia occurs
partially due to the nature of how our minds work and how we learn. Additionally, this is not to say
that all high-level guitar players are bad teachers. Expert amnesia, epistemology, and tying your
shoelaces. Let's talk briefly about how we learn. We learn by taking simple ideas and integrating
them into concepts. Then we learn more advanced ideas and skills by integrating concepts. For
example, we learn to identify the color brown, to identify the texture of wood and how to
distinguish shapes together. When we see a certain arrangement of this sensory data and we create the
mental concept of a chair, we learn what a chair is, what a table is and what a bench is, and we
integrate these low-level concepts to form a slightly higher-level concept of furniture.
Learning guitar works the same way, but we have the added complexity of performing a physical action in addition to building mental concepts.
There is a mechanical and a conceptual side to learning guitar, and they have to be worked on simultaneously.
As a guitar example, to pick through a three-note-per-string scale, we have to train three separate skills.
1. Picking notes on a single string.
2. Controlling how the pick travels between strings.
3. Visualizing the scale position on the guitar neck
and then combine them to effectively pick through a scale
Now, imagine it took you several months to master the two basic motions of picking on a single string
controlling the movement of the pick between strings
and visualizing guitar scales in different keys
Then, you relentlessly shred scales for 20 years
It's easy to imagine that you might have forgotten what it was like to work on the fundamental building blocks of your technique.
Another possibility is that the guitar player in question did not consciously distinguish between each element of picking through a scale.
They just did it a million times until something clicked, and they found they were able to shred their scales.
The advice someone in this situation would give, based on their experience, is that you just need to do it a million times.
And while there is certainly a strong element of repetition needed to develop a skill,
consciously identifying the components of that skill and working on them individually,
then integrating them will help you learn a lot, lot faster.
You have expert amnesia, too.
Take something you do every day, such as tying your shoelaces or brushing your teeth.
Now, write out a list of instructions on how to do that action.
Finally, follow your instructions exactly.
Would someone who had never performed that task before
be able to follow your instructions and accomplish the task?
If you wrote something like, just do it, then the answer is no,
and you have expert amnesia.
If you take 10, 15 minutes, sat and thought,
you could probably work out an effective list of instructions.
You will probably find that your instructions need some testing
to help you fully document the process of brushing your teeth.
Why do we get expert amnesia?
A fundamental part of what our brains do, and what learning is, is automating.
We consciously train a skill and over time, and with enough repetitions, we eventually automate that skill,
forgetting the fundamental components of the skill and retaining the higher-level outlook.
As an example, we go from having to visualize the scale, move the pick between the strings,
and carefully fret the notes to just playing a major scale. This is a natural and incredible
feature of how our minds work, which allows us to work on higher level concepts and more advanced
skills. Ideas and execution. This is quite a general idea we are going to look at. Someone
can explain an idea to you, and that idea may take two minutes to explain. It could take two months
or two years to execute and put into practice. For example, I can explain the fundamentals of
sweep picking to you in about 15 minutes, covering all the vital aspects of the technique.
Properly learning that technique will usually take six to nine months. Why is that? When we
are learning a technique, we are forcing neural pathways in our brain to grow and reinforce.
This is a physical process in our brain, and it takes time to happen. This may seem like a
simple concept, but it's important because often people think that because they understand an idea
but can't execute the idea on the spot, they cannot execute the idea at all. This is completely wrong.
Understand that your ability to understand an idea and perform the idea, while related,
exist on completely different timescales. If you can grasp this, you will save yourself a lot of
frustration. Perfection as a guide, one step farther as the goal. This is a concept that we
will revisit, possibly more than once, but I want to cover it here, as it is another big mindset
idea. Often when it comes to learning guitar, I see students try to get things perfect. Now,
I'm not saying don't try to get something perfect, but you have to understand that knowledge and
ability are not linear. We previously looked at this with the spiral theory of knowledge.
Perfection is a curse that can affect you in your practice and your composition. Let's look at both.
Perfection in your practice. Often, a student will want to be able to play an exercise perfectly
before moving on to the next exercise or next lesson. When you work this way, the 80-20 rule
starts to work against you. The 80-20 rule states that 80% of the results come from 20% of the work,
or in reverse, the top 20% of results take 80% of the work. In plain English, this means that
getting an exercise to 80% takes 20% of the work, and getting that last 20% takes 80% of the work.
That is, the last little bit of exercise to reach perfection takes four times as much work.
In general, I find that getting an exercise to around 80% to 90% and then moving on to the next
helps students progress much faster than if they spend all their time on getting one exercise to
100%. I also find that if a student is to practice this way for several weeks, they will find that
when they revisit an older exercise, they had at 80%. They can usually get it to 100% with relative
ease. As counterintuitive as this sounds, it is very effective. Perfection in your songwriting.
Songwriting is a very personal experience, and releasing a song can be incredibly stressful.
You're taking something you've worked on and putting it out to the world. This can be even
worse in the modern-day setting of the internet and social media, with trolls and haters lurking
in the void, waiting for the chance to tear down what you've put your work into. I've experienced
this myself. Before releasing my album Impetuous Desire, I listened to it every night before going
to sleep for a month, wondering if it was good enough and if I should just delete it. Fortunately,
I saw the light and released it. I know that students have felt anxiety about releasing music
they have composed. Maybe you can relate to how they feel. Where does this anxiety come from?
It can come from, one, comparing what we have composed and recorded to our favorite songs,
then concluding that our song falls short.
Two, wondering who we are to go and release a song.
Three, identifying any minute errors in the song that no one else will ever hear or be able to hear.
So when it comes to composing and releasing your music, what should the standard be?
We do want to seek perfection, but in our effort, not the product of our effort.
We can't guarantee that we will write a great song,
but we can guarantee that we will put 100% into it,
that we will apply ourselves in a focused way and throw everything we have at it.
That is the standard of perfection that we should adhere to.
Our job as composers is not to judge the output of our work,
that is for the public to do.
Our job is to judge the standard of the effort we put into our work
Additionally, consider this
If you try, you can probably write a song that is at least half decent
Is there one person in the world who will enjoy listening to that song?
Is there one person in the world who for a few minutes
You could make their life better by listening to your song?
Probably
Given the population of the world and how tragically awful most modern music is
This is almost certainly true
If you try and judge your music as good or bad, you will psychologically paralyze yourself.
So don't do it.
The speed you can work at increases with time.
When you are at the start of your journey, the time it takes to complete projects can seem daunting.
Your first instrumental song may take you months to complete.
You do some simple maths and extrapolate that it will take you three years to complete a short album.

That can be quite daunting. At this point, it's easy to feel that the mountain ahead of you is insurmountable. However, the above calculation fails to take into account how you will improve with time.

Sure, your first few songs will take you a few months to compose, but after that experience, you'll be able to compose a bit faster. You'll learn workflow hacks that you can use to use your software faster.
You'll learn more efficient ways to record.
You'll learn more efficient ways to learn your compositions.
If you keep studying, you will learn faster ways of composing.
You'll become more solid with your understanding of the fundamentals that go into composing,
speeding up the rate at which you can compose.
Your playing and performance skills will improve,
meaning that you no longer need 1,021 takes to get a good recording of that difficult lick.
If you just keep working at it consistently, you will slowly and consistently improve over time.
As we mentioned earlier, if you stick to the process for a few years,
you will find your ability to compose and record increases consistently,
allowing you to work faster at a higher quality than before.
The myth and danger of going all in.
You don't have to look far in the creative world to find the advice of going all in.
The gurus and experts peddle this, as well as their lackeys.
Why is this a myth, and why do people keep pushing this idea?
The myth.
Succeeding in any creative venture takes time and a bit of luck.
You can be a great composer, but there might not be an audience for what you create,
or if there is an audience, developing that audience may take time.
There is one inescapable truth.
You're going to need money to live.
You need a roof over your head and food on your table.
Other people create these things and you need to make money so that you can trade for them.
If you go all in, you find yourself with a lot of time, which is great for creating,
but without an income, which is not so great for living.
A more effective approach is to keep a day job so that you can pay for your life
and work on your composing as a side project until it takes off, if that's what you want.
Why does this myth keep going?
This myth is often perpetuated by the marketing gurus
as a way to guilt you into being serious about your music
and buying into their programs.
They'll roll out the story of the commander
who ordered his troops to burn their ships
to force them to win the battle.
Unfortunately, all that you get from this
is losing a big chunk of change
and putting yourself in a financially precarious position.
