paragraphs.ca: En què treballes a cada sessió de pràctica concreta? Ara que ja has planificat els teus objectius a llarg termini, una manera d'assolir-los i quan practicaràs, l'últim pas és pensar què practicaràs en aquestes sessions de pràctica programades.

paragraphs.en: In general, I recommend having three to seven things that you are working on with your playing at any one time. You want to ensure that your practice time is balanced appropriately, which is an ongoing skill.
paragraphs.ca: En general, recomano tenir entre tres i set coses en què treballar amb la teva manera de tocar en un moment donat. Has de procurar que el teu temps de pràctica estigui ben equilibrat, cosa que és una habilitat que es va desenvolupant.

paragraphs.en: Be careful with taking on more than seven things to practice. You will end up not being able to spend enough time on any one item to improve at it.
paragraphs.ca: Ves amb compte si agafes més de set coses per practicar. Acabaràs sense poder dedicar prou temps a cap d'elles per millorar-hi.

paragraphs.en: The perfect practice routine. I want to take a minute here to point out that there is no such thing as the perfect practice routine, only an appropriate practice routine for this point in time.
paragraphs.ca: La rutina de pràctica perfecta. Vull aturar-me un moment aquí per assenyalar que la rutina de pràctica perfecta no existeix; només hi ha una rutina de pràctica adequada per a aquest moment concret.

paragraphs.en: You will find that your practice routine changes and evolves as your abilities, goals and demands on your life change. Anyway, back to talking about practice.
paragraphs.ca: Descobriràs que la teva rutina de pràctica canvia i evoluciona a mesura que canvien les teves habilitats, els teus objectius i les exigències de la teva vida. En fi, tornem a parlar de la pràctica.

paragraphs.en: There are three ways you can consider organizing your practice time. 1. The rotating practice system. 2. AB system 3. 1. Item system The rotating practice system This system works best for people that are working on 3 to 7 different practice items, which are exercises to work on different skill sets, and the person in question also has a fluctuating amount of time that they can practice for each day.
paragraphs.ca: Hi ha tres maneres de plantejar l'organització del teu temps de pràctica. 1. El sistema de pràctica rotativa. 2. El sistema A-B. 3. El sistema d'un sol element. El sistema de pràctica rotativa. Aquest sistema funciona millor per a persones que treballen de 3 a 7 elements de pràctica diferents, que són exercicis per treballar diferents conjunts d'habilitats, i que a més tenen una quantitat de temps variable que poden dedicar a practicar cada dia.

paragraphs.en: We want to make sure that you can evenly practice all items. Let's say there are 7 things you want to practice. Practice items A, B, C, D, E, F, and G.
paragraphs.ca: Volem assegurar-nos que pots practicar tots els elements de manera uniforme. Diguem que hi ha 7 coses que vols practicar. Els elements de pràctica A, B, C, D, E, F i G.

paragraphs.en: Let's also say that your weekly practice schedule looks like this. Monday, 60 minutes. Tuesday, 15 minutes. Wednesday, 45 minutes.
paragraphs.ca: Diguem també que el teu horari setmanal de pràctica és així. Dilluns, 60 minuts. Dimarts, 15 minuts. Dimecres, 45 minuts.

paragraphs.en: Thursday, 15 minutes. Friday, 30 minutes. Saturday, 60 minutes. Sunday, 45 minutes. I would practice your items for 15 minutes each as follows.
paragraphs.ca: Dijous, 15 minuts. Divendres, 30 minuts. Dissabte, 60 minuts. Diumenge, 45 minuts. Jo practicaria els elements 15 minuts cadascun de la manera següent.

paragraphs.en: Monday, 60 minutes total, A, B, C, D. Tuesday, 15 minutes total, E. Wednesday, 45 minutes total, F, G, A. Thursday, 15 minutes total, B.
paragraphs.ca: Dilluns, 60 minuts en total, A, B, C, D. Dimarts, 15 minuts en total, E. Dimecres, 45 minuts en total, F, G, A. Dijous, 15 minuts en total, B.

paragraphs.en: Friday, 30 minutes total, C, D. Saturday, 60 minutes total, E, F, G, A. Sunday, 45 minutes total, B, C, D. This way, you rotate through your practice items evenly, ensuring that they all receive nearly the same attention.
paragraphs.ca: Divendres, 30 minuts en total, C, D. Dissabte, 60 minuts en total, E, F, G, A. Diumenge, 45 minuts en total, B, C, D. D'aquesta manera vas rotant pels teus elements de pràctica de manera uniforme, assegurant-te que tots reben gairebé la mateixa atenció.

paragraphs.en: You can physically organize this system by printing out or writing down your exercises. Have one page per exercise. Label each page if you want to and put them all on your music stand for practice.
paragraphs.ca: Pots organitzar aquest sistema físicament imprimint o escrivint els teus exercicis. Tingues una pàgina per exercici. Etiqueta cada pàgina si vols i posa-les totes al faristol per practicar.

paragraphs.en: Set your practice timer for 15 minutes and practice the exercise in front of you. When your timer goes off, move that exercise to the back of the pile.
paragraphs.ca: Posa el temporitzador de pràctica a 15 minuts i practica l'exercici que tens davant. Quan soni el temporitzador, passa aquell exercici al final de la pila.

paragraphs.en: Set your timer for 15 minutes and start on the next exercise. This system is incredibly simple and easy to follow. It allows you to sit down and get started with no preparation or fluffing around.
paragraphs.ca: Posa el temporitzador a 15 minuts i comença el següent exercici. Aquest sistema és increïblement senzill i fàcil de seguir. Et permet seure i posar-t'hi sense preparació ni donar voltes.

paragraphs.en: This system does not have to be rigid. When I was following this system several years ago, if I found myself having a breakthrough moment with a certain exercise and I was smashing my personal bests with the metronome, I would run with it for the rest of that practice session and see just how far I could go, then resume the rotation system the following day.
paragraphs.ca: Aquest sistema no ha de ser rígid. Quan jo seguia aquest sistema fa uns quants anys, si em trobava tenint un moment de revelació amb un exercici determinat i estava superant els meus rècords personals amb el metrònom, ho aprofitava durant la resta d'aquella sessió de pràctica i veia fins on podia arribar, i després reprenia el sistema de rotació l'endemà.

paragraphs.en: A-B system. This is effective for people that want to work on several areas of their playing and have a consistent practice schedule where they can practice for roughly the same amount of time each day.
paragraphs.ca: El sistema A-B. És eficaç per a persones que volen treballar diverses àrees de la seva manera de tocar i que tenen un horari de pràctica constant, en què poden practicar aproximadament el mateix temps cada dia.

paragraphs.en: You break up your practice items into Day A items and Day B items, and you're alternate between the two. For example, you could have technique exercises on Day A and a song you are learning to focus on for Day B.
paragraphs.ca: Divideixes els teus elements de pràctica en elements del dia A i elements del dia B, i vas alternant entre els dos. Per exemple, podries tenir exercicis de tècnica el dia A i una cançó que estàs aprenent per centrar-t'hi el dia B.

paragraphs.en: This practice schedule allows you to work a little deeper on certain items than the rotating system.
paragraphs.ca: Aquest horari de pràctica et permet treballar una mica més a fons certs elements que amb el sistema rotatiu.

paragraphs.en: 1. Item System If you are practicing for a gig or a recording session, then you will want to distribute your time differently, focusing on the project that you have to complete. Maybe you'll be putting 75% of your practice time into practicing songs and only 25% into working on your technique. For this system, nearly all your time goes into practicing for the project. I would still put some time, even if it is not much,
paragraphs.ca: El sistema d'un sol element. Si estàs practicant per a un concert o una sessió de gravació, voldràs distribuir el temps d'una manera diferent, centrant-te en el projecte que has de completar. Potser dedicaràs el 75 % del teu temps de pràctica a practicar cançons i només el 25 % a treballar la tècnica. Amb aquest sistema, gairebé tot el temps se'n va a practicar per al projecte. Jo encara hi dedicaria una mica de temps, encara que no fos gaire,

paragraphs.en: into working on technique and other skills, even if it is just a warm-up exercise or two. Which system is right for you?
paragraphs.ca: a treballar la tècnica i altres habilitats, encara que només sigui un exercici d'escalfament o dos. Quin sistema és el millor per a tu?

paragraphs.en: We've outlined three different systems for organizing your practice. You'll have to decide which one is best for you. Pick one system and stick to it for two to three months, then change it as you see necessary.
paragraphs.ca: Hem descrit tres sistemes diferents per organitzar la teva pràctica. Hauràs de decidir quin és el millor per a tu. Tria un sistema i mantén-lo durant dos o tres mesos, i després canvia'l quan ho vegis necessari.

paragraphs.en: You don't have to stick to one system for the rest of your life, but you do want to stick to it for at least two to three months.
paragraphs.ca: No cal que et mantinguis en un sol sistema la resta de la teva vida, però sí que convé mantenir-lo almenys dos o tres mesos.

paragraphs.en: You can create hybrids of these systems. As with anything, think about what it is you're trying to achieve. Figure out a way to do that.
paragraphs.ca: Pots crear híbrids d'aquests sistemes. Com amb tot, pensa què és el que intentes aconseguir. Troba una manera de fer-ho.

paragraphs.en: Try a system out for a couple of months and then assess how it's going.
paragraphs.ca: Prova un sistema durant un parell de mesos i després valora com va.

paragraphs.en: Feedback and improvement. Whatever you are practicing, you want to be aware of what it is you are doing. As obvious as that sounds, it can be surprisingly difficult.
paragraphs.ca: Retroalimentació i millora. Sigui el que sigui que practiquis, has de ser conscient del que estàs fent. Per obvi que soni, pot ser sorprenentment difícil.

paragraphs.en: When you are focusing on trying to move your fingers in a certain way with something a bit new, it can be difficult to really listen to what you are doing and observe those motions objectively.
paragraphs.ca: Quan et concentres a intentar moure els dits d'una manera determinada amb alguna cosa una mica nova, pot ser difícil escoltar de debò què estàs fent i observar aquests moviments amb objectivitat.

paragraphs.en: There will be things that you are aware of and also things that you are not aware of. One benefit to having a teacher is you get instant feedback on what you are doing.
paragraphs.ca: Hi haurà coses de les quals siguis conscient i també coses de les quals no ho siguis. Un avantatge de tenir un professor és que obtens retroalimentació immediata sobre què estàs fent.

paragraphs.en: Another highly effective method of getting feedback is to record yourself. This will allow you to focus on listening so you can dissect what you are doing and figure out which bits of an exercise need the most work.
paragraphs.ca: Un altre mètode molt eficaç per obtenir retroalimentació és gravar-te. Això et permetrà centrar-te a escoltar per poder diseccionar què estàs fent i esbrinar quines parts d'un exercici necessiten més feina.

paragraphs.en: You will also find it beneficial to keep a short log of your practice. Record things like the maximum tempos that you reach and mistakes you are making.
paragraphs.ca: També et serà útil portar un registre breu de la teva pràctica. Anota coses com els tempos màxims que assoleixes i els errors que comets.

paragraphs.en: Is there a particular point of an exercise that you are consistently struggling with? A chord change that is a bit ropey?
paragraphs.ca: Hi ha algun punt concret d'un exercici amb què t'encalles de manera consistent? Un canvi d'acord que sona una mica maldestre?

paragraphs.en: Whatever feedback you are getting, whether it's from a teacher or your own video audio recording, make notes on it in your practice log.
paragraphs.ca: Sigui quina sigui la retroalimentació que rebis, tant si és d'un professor com de la teva pròpia gravació de vídeo o d'àudio, pren notes al teu registre de pràctica.

paragraphs.en: If you have printed your exercises on paper, you can keep a practice log on the back of each sheet. This way, when you next come to that practice item, you will know what it is you need to focus on.
paragraphs.ca: Si has imprès els exercicis en paper, pots portar un registre de pràctica al darrere de cada full. Així, quan tornis a aquell element de pràctica, sabràs en què t'has de centrar.

paragraphs.en: This also stops you from fiddling around with computer programs and keeps you focused on the task at hand. We will look at specific practice techniques later in the book.
paragraphs.ca: Això també evita que et distreguis amb programes d'ordinador i et manté centrat en la tasca que tens entre mans. Més endavant al llibre veurem tècniques de pràctica concretes.

paragraphs.en: How much should you practice? Practicing more is better than practicing less. If you want to play at the highest levels, then you'll need to be practicing for a few hours a day, at least three.
paragraphs.ca: Quant hauries de practicar? Practicar més és millor que practicar menys. Si vols tocar al més alt nivell, hauràs de practicar unes quantes hores al dia, com a mínim tres.

paragraphs.en: Steve Vai was famous for his immense nine-hour guitar workout that he used to do. Michelangelo Battio would practice his picking for two hours every day to develop the insane speed he achieved.
paragraphs.ca: Steve Vai era famós per la seva immensa sessió de guitarra de nou hores que solia fer. Michelangelo Battio practicava la pua dues hores cada dia per desenvolupar la velocitat increïble que va assolir.

paragraphs.en: Ingwi Malmsteen would fall asleep with his guitar in his hands. If you want to be at the top levels of playing, that's what it takes.
paragraphs.ca: Ingwi Malmsteen s'adormia amb la guitarra a les mans. Si vols estar al més alt nivell de la interpretació, això és el que cal.

paragraphs.en: If you're a beginner, you want to build up your practice time over a period of weeks to months, going from practicing for 10 minutes a day to practicing for 10 hours a day will result in injury.
paragraphs.ca: Si ets principiant, has d'anar augmentant el temps de pràctica al llarg de setmanes o mesos; passar de practicar 10 minuts al dia a practicar 10 hores al dia acabarà en una lesió.

paragraphs.en: Practicing for extended periods is very taxing on the nerves, tendons and ligaments, and by increasing practice time over a longer period, you give the body a chance to strengthen these connective tissues.
paragraphs.ca: Practicar durant períodes prolongats desgasta molt els nervis, els tendons i els lligaments, i si augmentes el temps de pràctica al llarg d'un període més llarg dones al cos l'oportunitat de reforçar aquests teixits connectius.

paragraphs.en: If you are wanting to increase your practice time, do so in 15-minute increments, a week at a time. If you want to increase your practice time faster, add extra practice time at opposite ends of the day.
paragraphs.ca: Si vols augmentar el teu temps de pràctica, fes-ho en increments de 15 minuts, una setmana cada vegada. Si vols augmentar el temps de pràctica més de pressa, afegeix temps extra de pràctica en els extrems oposats del dia.

paragraphs.en: For example, if you practice for an hour in the morning, you could add a 30-minute practice session in the evening. By practicing at opposite ends of the day, you give the body a chance to rest between sessions.
paragraphs.ca: Per exemple, si practiques una hora al matí, podries afegir una sessió de pràctica de 30 minuts al vespre. Practicant en els extrems oposats del dia, dones al cos l'oportunitat de descansar entre sessions.

paragraphs.en: You also want to take micro-breaks when practicing. For every repetition of an exercise, take 5 seconds to consciously relax your arms and hands.
paragraphs.ca: També has de fer microdescansos quan practiques. Per cada repetició d'un exercici, dedica 5 segons a relaxar conscientment els braços i les mans.

paragraphs.en: Every 10, 15 minutes, take a break, get up and walk for 10 seconds before getting started on the next practice item. Once a week, I like to take a day off from practicing to let my body rest.
paragraphs.ca: Cada 10 o 15 minuts, fes una pausa, aixeca't i camina 10 segons abans de començar el següent element de pràctica. Un cop a la setmana, m'agrada fer un dia de descans de la pràctica per deixar reposar el cos.

paragraphs.en: I'll also take days off as needed. For example, yesterday I was practicing and started feeling a bit sore, so I took the rest of the day off from practicing.
paragraphs.ca: També em prenc dies lliures quan cal. Per exemple, ahir estava practicant i vaig començar a notar una mica de dolor, així que vaig descansar la resta del dia.

paragraphs.en: Warning signs of injury. This and the following sections are not medical advice, just my experience. It is possible to injure yourself from playing the guitar.
paragraphs.ca: Senyals d'alerta de lesió. Aquesta secció i les següents no són consells mèdics, només la meva experiència. És possible lesionar-se tocant la guitarra.

paragraphs.en: This can be caused by practicing too much, and having bad technique can make this worse. See the appendix for the correct way to sit with your guitar.
paragraphs.ca: Això ho pot causar practicar massa, i tenir una mala tècnica ho pot empitjorar. Consulta l'apèndix per veure la manera correcta de seure amb la guitarra.

paragraphs.en: Common injuries that guitar players get are tennis elbow and carpal tunnel syndrome. These are both quite serious problems that can be permanent.
paragraphs.ca: Les lesions més habituals dels guitarristes són el colze de tennista i la síndrome del túnel carpià. Tots dos són problemes força greus que poden ser permanents.

paragraphs.en: More often than not, our body warns us before becoming injured, and it is important to be able to spot these warning signs.
paragraphs.ca: La majoria de les vegades, el nostre cos ens avisa abans de lesionar-se, i és important saber detectar aquests senyals d'alerta.

paragraphs.en: If your fingertips are sore, that is okay. While I don't recommend it, you can lose skin and get blisters on your fingertips, and while uncomfortable, this will heal. If you ever feel shooting pains, stabbing pains, like someone has stabbed you with a pointy pencil, burning sensations or pins and needles, then you need to stop playing immediately and not play for the rest of the day. Usually, resting for the day, and maybe the next day, will leave you feeling fine. Bathing the problem area
paragraphs.ca: Si tens la punta dels dits adolorida, no passa res. Tot i que no ho recomano, pots perdre pell i fer-te ampolles a la punta dels dits i, tot i que és incòmode, es curarà. Si mai notes dolors punxants, com si algú t'hagués clavat un llapis esmolat, sensacions de cremor o formigueig, aleshores has de parar de tocar immediatament i no tocar la resta del dia. Normalment, descansar aquell dia, i potser el següent, et farà sentir bé. Banyar la zona afectada

paragraphs.en: in icy cold water for a few minutes after practice can help recovery. Avoiding injury. Doing a light yoga routine before and after practice can help prevent injuries. There are books and DVDs available on Amazon that cover yoga for musicians. Any of them are probably fine.
paragraphs.ca: en aigua molt freda durant uns minuts després de practicar pot ajudar a la recuperació. Evitar les lesions. Fer una rutina de ioga suau abans i després de practicar pot ajudar a prevenir lesions. Hi ha llibres i DVD disponibles a Amazon que tracten el ioga per a músics. Qualsevol d'ells probablement està bé.

paragraphs.en: I've used a DVD called Yoga for Musicians by Penelope Roskell which I found very effective at a time when I was recovering from an injury When practicing, take lots of little breaks In the section on how to use a metronome properly I advise that you have a bar of count-in between repetitions of exercises In addition to refocusing your mind and figuring out where the count is You can use this as an opportunity to purposely relax your arms and hands before the next repetition starts.
paragraphs.ca: He fet servir un DVD titulat Yoga for Musicians, de Penelope Roskell, que em va semblar molt eficaç en un moment en què m'estava recuperant d'una lesió. Quan practiquis, fes moltes pauses curtes. A la secció sobre com fer servir el metrònom correctament, aconsello tenir un compàs de compte enrere entre repeticions dels exercicis. A més de tornar a centrar la ment i esbrinar on és el compte, pots aprofitar-ho per relaxar deliberadament els braços i les mans abans que comenci la repetició següent.

paragraphs.en: Every 15 minutes, put the guitar down for a few minutes and have a stretch. Walk to the kitchen and back or something to get your body moving a little.
paragraphs.ca: Cada 15 minuts, deixa la guitarra uns minuts i estira't. Vés a la cuina i torna, o alguna cosa així, per moure una mica el cos.

paragraphs.en: Again, when you start feeling warning signs of injury, put the guitar down. Never play through the pain. That is a stupid thing to do.
paragraphs.ca: De nou, quan comencis a notar senyals d'alerta de lesió, deixa la guitarra. No toquis mai amb dolor. És una cosa estúpida de fer.

paragraphs.en: I know because I have made that mistake several times in the past, including one injury which meant taking several months off from playing the guitar so that I could recover, during which my arm was almost unusable. If you do any tasks in your daily life that have a risk of RSI, such as a lot of typing, then research proper posture and technique to avoid repetitive injury.
paragraphs.ca: Ho sé perquè he comès aquest error diverses vegades en el passat, incloent-hi una lesió que em va obligar a estar diversos mesos sense tocar la guitarra per poder-me recuperar, durant els quals el braç era gairebé inservible. Si fas tasques a la teva vida diària que comporten risc de lesions per esforç repetitiu, com ara escriure molt amb el teclat, informa't sobre la postura i la tècnica correctes per evitar lesions per repetició.

paragraphs.en: Make sure you take breaks. This will take some strain off your connective tissues, and they won't be quite as tired when it comes to practicing the guitar.
paragraphs.ca: Assegura't de fer pauses. Això traurà una mica de tensió dels teus teixits connectius i no estaran tan cansats a l'hora de practicar la guitarra.

paragraphs.en: Recovering from injury. If you do find yourself injured, seek help from a professional. I find
paragraphs.ca: Recuperar-se d'una lesió. Si et trobes lesionat, busca ajuda d'un professional. Trobo

chapters.title_ca: En què treballes a cada sessió de pràctica?

segments.text: Recovering from injury. If you do find yourself injured, seek help from a professional. I find
that locating a good physiotherapist that specializes in musicians is the most effective
treatment, depending on the injury. The injuries I've had to deal with have all been things that
a physiotherapist specializes in. Going private, if possible, is almost always better than waiting
for government-provided health care as you can be seen, diagnosed, and start treatment almost
immediately, rather than waiting for months on end. Going private can be expensive, but if possible,
it is worth the cost. You may want to seek two or three professional opinions before deciding on a
course of action. When I had my first serious guitar injury, I saw three professionals. The
first recommended cortisol injections in my elbow. The next wanted to do a risky surgery to cut a
piece of bone from my elbow. The next recommended a course of stretching, physiotherapy, and yoga,
mixed with some ultrasound treatment. I started with the lowest risk recommendation, stretching,
physio and yoga, which fix me up nicely within a few weeks. A professional is always going to
speak from experience. Surgeons know how surgery works, so if you see a surgeon,
they'll recommend surgery. For some reason, the medical profession doesn't seem to be too aware
of what physiotherapy can offer in terms of healing a patient. Whenever I get an injury,
my physiotherapist is the first port of call.
How to make your practice time as effective as possible
So far we have discussed a lot of ideas around practice,
but now we are going to dig into some of the tools, techniques and approaches you can use while practicing
that will make your practice time as effective as possible.
Use a metronome
If you are not playing with a metronome, you are not playing in time, and playing in time is important.
We need to use a metronome because something every musician struggles with,
guitar players included, is perceiving time accurately.
As an example, go back to the start of this article and try and count to 10 while reading it.
Or stop reading after 10 seconds. Pretty tricky, right?
We face a similar problem when playing the guitar, especially if we are working on new material.
Keeping track of time while our mind is focused on something we are learning is incredibly difficult.
I'm sure you've experienced working on some new chords,
and you slip out of time without realizing it when the chord changes come around.
The metronome gives us an external reference to make sure that our timing is accurate.
What is the purpose of using a metronome?
Often, guitarists think that the purpose of using a metronome to practice is to play faster.
This is sort of true, but not quite.
The goal of using a metronome when practicing the guitar is to play more accurately.
And once you can play accurately, you will find your speed naturally increases.
Think of speed as a byproduct of accurate playing.
Speed is a byproduct of accuracy.
If you want to play guitar faster, learn to play more accurately.
There are several things involved with reaching high speeds with your lead guitar playing,
and accurate timing is one of the most important.
Side note, you can check how fast you can play the guitar with our guitar speed calculator
There is a second element to using a metronome
In addition to wanting to practice playing accurately, we want to become comfortable at that tempo
When learning to play a piece or exercise, we want to be able to play feeling relaxed,
not tensed up, and not pushing the very limit of our ability.
Once we have achieved a level of comfort and reliability,
i.e. being able to play the same exercise two-three times in a row without making mistakes,
we can then increase the tempo.
So to summarize, our two goals with using a metronome are
1. To play more accurately
2. To become comfortable at a certain tempo.
The top 10 mistakes guitarists make when using a metronome.
Here are some common mistakes that guitar players make when using a metronome,
along with solutions that you can use today to help make your guitar practice more effective.
Mistake 1. Not listening to the metronome.
This might be an obvious one, but you would be surprised how often it happens.
It is mainly a problem for beginner guitar players who aren't used to practicing with a metronome.
When you use a metronome, you have to do two things at once, listen and play the guitar.
And doing these two things at once can be difficult.
It's common for a beginner to turn their metronome on, start practicing,
and the second they are playing the guitar, they stop listening to the metronome,
quickly going out of time, or they'll play with the metronome for a few clicks
and then phase it out in their mind. Now, listening to a metronome and playing the guitar
at the same time can be quite challenging, but make the mental push to listen to that metronome
while you're playing. Solution. Push your mental focus to the limit. Mental focus is like a muscle.
It will improve with timing. The more you try, the easier it will become. Slow things down so it is
easier to focus on all the things you need to do at the same time. Jim Rohn has a great quote on
this. Don't wish it were easier. Wish you were better. But don't wish practice. Mistake too.
Not leaving breaks between repetitions. This sort of ties into the previous problem.
Sometimes when working on an exercise, a guitarist will use the metronome,
they will be listening to it, and they will be playing repetitions of the exercise back to back.
The problem with this is that after a few repetitions, it is quite easy to lose mental focus on listening and playing,
and you slip into just playing without listening to the metronome.
Let's illustrate this idea with some tab.
Let's say we were playing the following exercise.
Figure 3, tab example.
A simple exercise to work through the first position of the A minor pentatonic scale from the root note on the fourth string.
Now, when practicing repetitions of this exercise, some guitar players may approach it as follows.
Figure 4. Tab example.
This is the same exercise as above, being played three times in a row.
I recommend you do not take this approach when practicing scales.
If you look through the tab and compare it to the three-bar example that preceded it,
you can see that we have taken the scale example and are playing it three times in a row.
I recommend you do not do this. It is easy to lose focus and slip out of time with the metronome.
Often when beginners slip out of time, they cannot get back in time, and then continue to play,
out of time to the metronome. A better way to approach this exercise is as follows.
Figure 5. Tab example. Here we have placed a bar of rests between each repetition.
This is a much more sensible way to practice a scale.
If you look at the above tab, you can see that we have placed a bar of rests between each repetition.
This gives you a chance to refocus and count yourself back in.
This helps ensure that you're playing each repetition nicely in time with the metronome.
If you need to take two bars or three bars of rest before you come back in, take it.
There is no need to rush.
Solution
When practicing an exercise to the metronome, make sure you give yourself a little break between repetitions.
This break only needs to be a few seconds, during which you can refocus yourself and come back in.
Mistake 3. Starting to play.
Without listening to 3, 4 clicks, or counting yourself in.
Another common mistake is to put the metronome on and start playing immediately.
When students do this, they never come in on time.
It is physically impossible to come in on time if you do this.
Let's think about it for a minute.
The metronome is used to measure the passage of time.
To measure the passage of time, you need a starting point and an end point.
You need to hear two clicks, at the very least.
If you have only heard one click, it is impossible to know when the second click will be,
and most of us will have to hear three, four clicks to get a good feel for the timing.
So by coming in too soon, you are guaranteeing that you will not be playing in time to the metronome.
Solution.
When you practice to a metronome, give yourself a four-beat count in
or whatever is appropriate for the meter you are playing in.
Mistake four.
Not counting out loud to the metronome.
This is a weird one.
If ever there was one weird secret to improving your guitar playing, this was it.
When I first started teaching, I noticed some students would struggle to play in time to a metronome,
even when playing something that was well within their ability level and at a slow tempo.
For whatever reason, they struggled to count to the metronome and play the guitar using only their internal monologue.
I found that when I made them count out loud to the metronome, their timing improved dramatically,
often playing exercises close to perfect after they had been butchering it just ten seconds prior.
I use this myself all the time when learning something new.
Sometimes it can be quite tricky to get the hang of talking out loud and playing the guitar at the same time,
but I guarantee if you put in the time to practice it, it will dramatically improve your timing and accuracy.
Solution. Always count out loud when practicing with a metronome. When counting out loud,
count confidently. Don't whisper or mumble. Mistake 5. Not understanding the count of what
they are playing. Maybe we should have made this an earlier mistake in the list. A vital part of
using a metronome effectively is to understand the count of the music that you are playing.
What we mean by this is, are we counting 1, 2, 3, 4 to the metronome, or 1 and 2 and 3 and 4, or 1e and r2e and...
R3E and R4E and R or 1-2-3-2-2-3-3-2-3-4-2-3 or some other method of counting. Understanding this requires an understanding of rhythm.
Solution. Study the theory of rhythm and learn how to count various rhythms. Make sure you can take any rhythm and dissect it.
Mistake 6. Not using the metronome to count every note.
This is a mistake I certainly made when I was younger.
I would often use my metronome to count the beat, usually quarter notes.
However, this means that when it comes to playing subdivisions,
eighth notes, sixteenths, etc.,
I was effectively guessing, sometimes more accurately than others.
For example, if I was playing a section in sixteenths
and the metronome was counting quarter notes,
how would I know if the sixteenths that fall between the beat
are being played precisely? I wouldn't. Solution. Have your metronome count the smallest subdivision
that you are playing. If you are playing an exercise that has sixteenths, make sure the
metronome is counting sixteenths. If you are playing something that moves between various
subdivisions, consider programming a custom metronome in Guitar Pro, MuseScore, Logic Pro,
etc. Mistake 7. Not counting the start of the bar. This is different to mistake 3,
so please read on. Another common problem is that, after setting the metronome to count the beat or
smallest subdivision that they are playing, the student starts playing, gets distracted with a
tricky section, and an extra metronome click sneaks past without them realizing. This is especially
common when working on a difficult chord change. Maybe you've experienced this. You're strumming
away, perfectly in time to the metronome. The chord change comes up. It's a difficult one,
and while you are focusing on moving your fingers to the correct positions, an extra metronome
click sneaks past without you realizing. Now there are various techniques we can use to improve your
chord changes, which we'll cover later. However, there is a nice simple trick we can use with the
metronome to help us catch this mistake when it crops up. Like a lot of things in life,
awareness is half the battle. Solution. Make sure the metronome has a different sounding click
on beat one of the bar. After changing the metronome click, you'll know that if you are
halfway through a bar and you hear the beat one click, you have messed up and you need to go back
and figure out what went wrong and where. Mistake 8. Not keeping a record of your metronome tempos.
When practicing with a metronome, you will be playing the same exercise for several days
or even weeks trying to incrementally increase your accuracy and tempos. It is well worth keeping
a practice log of your tempos and any difficulties you encounter. At the end of each practice session,
make a note of the tempo you started at, the tempo you reached, and any notes you want to
remind yourself of for your practice session tomorrow. Maybe you need to make a note that
a particular section of an exercise had some string noise that you need to fix,
or a fret hand jump that you need to isolate to play correctly.

How to make your practice time as effective as possible So far we have discussed a lot of ideas around practice, but now we are going to dig into some of the tools, techniques and approaches you can use while practicing that will make your practice time as effective as possible.
paragraphs.ca: el meu fisioterapeuta és la primera parada. Com fer que el teu temps de pràctica sigui tan efectiu com sigui possible. Fins ara hem parlat de moltes idees sobre la pràctica, però ara ens endinsarem en algunes de les eines, tècniques i enfocaments que pots fer servir mentre practiques i que faran que el teu temps de pràctica sigui tan efectiu com sigui possible.

paragraphs.en: Use a metronome If you are not playing with a metronome, you are not playing in time, and playing in time is important. We need to use a metronome because something every musician struggles with, guitar players included, is perceiving time accurately.
paragraphs.ca: Fes servir un metrònom. Si no toques amb metrònom, no toques a temps, i tocar a temps és important. Hem de fer servir un metrònom perquè una cosa amb què lluita tot músic, guitarristes inclosos, és percebre el temps amb precisió.

paragraphs.en: As an example, go back to the start of this article and try and count to 10 while reading it. Or stop reading after 10 seconds. Pretty tricky, right?
paragraphs.ca: Com a exemple, torna a l'inici d'aquest article i intenta comptar fins a 10 mentre el llegeixes. O deixa de llegir al cap de 10 segons. Força complicat, oi?

paragraphs.en: We face a similar problem when playing the guitar, especially if we are working on new material. Keeping track of time while our mind is focused on something we are learning is incredibly difficult.
paragraphs.ca: Ens enfrontem a un problema semblant quan toquem la guitarra, sobretot si treballem material nou. Mantenir el control del temps mentre la ment està centrada en una cosa que estem aprenent és increïblement difícil.

paragraphs.en: I'm sure you've experienced working on some new chords, and you slip out of time without realizing it when the chord changes come around.
paragraphs.ca: Segur que has viscut això de treballar uns acords nous i perdre el temps sense adonar-te'n quan arriben els canvis d'acord.

paragraphs.en: The metronome gives us an external reference to make sure that our timing is accurate. What is the purpose of using a metronome?
paragraphs.ca: El metrònom ens dona una referència externa per assegurar-nos que el nostre tempo és precís. Quina és la finalitat de fer servir un metrònom?

paragraphs.en: Often, guitarists think that the purpose of using a metronome to practice is to play faster. This is sort of true, but not quite.
paragraphs.ca: Sovint, els guitarristes pensen que la finalitat de fer servir un metrònom per practicar és tocar més de pressa. És més o menys cert, però no ben bé.

paragraphs.en: The goal of using a metronome when practicing the guitar is to play more accurately. And once you can play accurately, you will find your speed naturally increases.
paragraphs.ca: L'objectiu de fer servir un metrònom quan practiques la guitarra és tocar amb més precisió. I un cop saps tocar amb precisió, veuràs que la teva velocitat augmenta de manera natural.

paragraphs.en: Think of speed as a byproduct of accurate playing. Speed is a byproduct of accuracy. If you want to play guitar faster, learn to play more accurately.
paragraphs.ca: Pensa en la velocitat com un efecte secundari de tocar amb precisió. La velocitat és un efecte secundari de la precisió. Si vols tocar la guitarra més de pressa, aprèn a tocar amb més precisió.

paragraphs.en: There are several things involved with reaching high speeds with your lead guitar playing, and accurate timing is one of the most important.
paragraphs.ca: Hi ha diverses coses implicades a assolir velocitats altes amb la guitarra solista, i un tempo precís és una de les més importants.

paragraphs.en: Side note, you can check how fast you can play the guitar with our guitar speed calculator There is a second element to using a metronome In addition to wanting to practice playing accurately, we want to become comfortable at that tempo When learning to play a piece or exercise, we want to be able to play feeling relaxed, not tensed up, and not pushing the very limit of our ability.
paragraphs.ca: Nota al marge: pots comprovar com de ràpid saps tocar la guitarra amb la nostra calculadora de velocitat de guitarra. Hi ha un segon element en fer servir un metrònom. A més de voler practicar tocant amb precisió, volem sentir-nos còmodes amb aquell tempo. Quan aprenem a tocar una peça o un exercici, volem poder tocar amb sensació de relaxació, no tensos, i no empenyent el límit màxim de la nostra capacitat.

paragraphs.en: Once we have achieved a level of comfort and reliability, i.e. being able to play the same exercise two-three times in a row without making mistakes, we can then increase the tempo.
paragraphs.ca: Un cop hem assolit un nivell de comoditat i fiabilitat, és a dir, poder tocar el mateix exercici dues o tres vegades seguides sense cometre errors, podem augmentar el tempo.

paragraphs.en: So to summarize, our two goals with using a metronome are 1. To play more accurately 2. To become comfortable at a certain tempo.
paragraphs.ca: Així, per resumir, els nostres dos objectius en fer servir un metrònom són: 1. Tocar amb més precisió. 2. Sentir-nos còmodes amb un tempo determinat.

paragraphs.en: The top 10 mistakes guitarists make when using a metronome. Here are some common mistakes that guitar players make when using a metronome, along with solutions that you can use today to help make your guitar practice more effective.
paragraphs.ca: Els 10 errors principals que cometen els guitarristes quan fan servir un metrònom. Aquí tens alguns errors habituals que cometen els guitarristes quan fan servir un metrònom, juntament amb solucions que pots aplicar avui mateix per fer que la teva pràctica de guitarra sigui més efectiva.

paragraphs.en: Mistake 1. Not listening to the metronome. This might be an obvious one, but you would be surprised how often it happens.
paragraphs.ca: Error 1. No escoltar el metrònom. Pot semblar obvi, però t'enduries una sorpresa de la freqüència amb què passa.

paragraphs.en: It is mainly a problem for beginner guitar players who aren't used to practicing with a metronome. When you use a metronome, you have to do two things at once, listen and play the guitar.
paragraphs.ca: És sobretot un problema per a guitarristes principiants que no estan acostumats a practicar amb metrònom. Quan fas servir un metrònom, has de fer dues coses alhora: escoltar i tocar la guitarra.

paragraphs.en: And doing these two things at once can be difficult. It's common for a beginner to turn their metronome on, start practicing, and the second they are playing the guitar, they stop listening to the metronome, quickly going out of time, or they'll play with the metronome for a few clicks and then phase it out in their mind. Now, listening to a metronome and playing the guitar at the same time can be quite challenging, but make the mental push to listen to that metronome
paragraphs.ca: I fer aquestes dues coses alhora pot ser difícil. És habitual que un principiant engegui el metrònom, comenci a practicar i, en el moment que està tocant la guitarra, deixi d'escoltar el metrònom, perdent el temps de seguida, o que toqui amb el metrònom uns quants clics i després el desconnecti mentalment. Ara bé, escoltar un metrònom i tocar la guitarra alhora pot ser força difícil, però fes l'esforç mental d'escoltar aquell metrònom

paragraphs.en: while you're playing. Solution. Push your mental focus to the limit. Mental focus is like a muscle. It will improve with timing. The more you try, the easier it will become. Slow things down so it is easier to focus on all the things you need to do at the same time. Jim Rohn has a great quote on this. Don't wish it were easier. Wish you were better. But don't wish practice. Mistake too.
paragraphs.ca: mentre toques. Solució. Empeny el teu focus mental fins al límit. El focus mental és com un múscul. Millorarà amb el temps. Com més ho intentes, més fàcil es fa. Alenteix les coses perquè sigui més fàcil centrar-te en tot el que has de fer alhora. Jim Rohn té una gran cita sobre això: «No desitgis que fos més fàcil. Desitja ser millor». Però no desitgis la pràctica. Error 2.

paragraphs.en: Not leaving breaks between repetitions. This sort of ties into the previous problem. Sometimes when working on an exercise, a guitarist will use the metronome, they will be listening to it, and they will be playing repetitions of the exercise back to back.
paragraphs.ca: No deixar pauses entre repeticions. Això es relaciona d'alguna manera amb el problema anterior. De vegades, quan treballa un exercici, un guitarrista fa servir el metrònom, l'escolta i toca repeticions de l'exercici una darrere l'altra.

paragraphs.en: The problem with this is that after a few repetitions, it is quite easy to lose mental focus on listening and playing, and you slip into just playing without listening to the metronome.
paragraphs.ca: El problema d'això és que, després d'unes quantes repeticions, és força fàcil perdre el focus mental en escoltar i tocar, i acabes tocant sense escoltar el metrònom.

paragraphs.en: Let's illustrate this idea with some tab. Let's say we were playing the following exercise. Figure 3, tab example. A simple exercise to work through the first position of the A minor pentatonic scale from the root note on the fourth string.

paragraphs.en: Solution When practicing an exercise to the metronome, make sure you give yourself a little break between repetitions. This break only needs to be a few seconds, during which you can refocus yourself and come back in.

paragraphs.en: Mistake 3. Starting to play. Without listening to 3, 4 clicks, or counting yourself in. Another common mistake is to put the metronome on and start playing immediately.

paragraphs.en: When students do this, they never come in on time. It is physically impossible to come in on time if you do this. Let's think about it for a minute.

paragraphs.en: You need to hear two clicks, at the very least. If you have only heard one click, it is impossible to know when the second click will be, and most of us will have to hear three, four clicks to get a good feel for the timing.
paragraphs.ca: Has de sentir dos clics, com a mínim. Si només n'has sentit un, és impossible saber quan arribarà el segon, i la majoria haurem de sentir tres o quatre clics per fer-nos una bona idea del tempo.

paragraphs.en: So by coming in too soon, you are guaranteeing that you will not be playing in time to the metronome. Solution. When you practice to a metronome, give yourself a four-beat count in or whatever is appropriate for the meter you are playing in.

Now, we are going to look at a collection of other techniques you can use to enhance your guitar practice.
Memorization
Often when working on an exercise, students will read the exercise as they are playing it.
If this is you, you will find it much more effective to memorize what you're working on rather than trying to read it.
If you are reading an exercise, your brain has to deal with visually processing the music on the page,
and then it tells your body to play the notes on your guitar.
If you memorize that piece of music, then you can eliminate the mental process of reading the music, which allows you to completely focus on playing the music.
Play exactly the same way every time.
A common practice mistake students make is to use different fingers when playing a certain section of an exercise.
For example, they might play a particular note using the first finger,
and then the next time they play that note, they use their second finger.
This is a huge mistake.
One of the goals of practicing is to train our muscle memory to learn specific movements
so that we don't have to consciously struggle with every note that we play.
We are programming our subconscious on how to play something.
To do this, we have to repeat the exact same motion hundreds of times in a row.
When you use random fingers to play an exercise, rather than training that one exercise into your muscle memory,
you are training your muscle memory on four, five, nine or even more different exercises simultaneously,
which is not very helpful.
As you can imagine, this means it takes four, five, nine times as long to learn that piece of music.
This is a big reason why a lot of guitar players struggle to make progress.
So if you would like to learn faster, make a specific choice about what fingers you're going to use and stick to it.
If you need to, write the fingers down on the tab you are using.
As a side note, one of the benefits of studying scales is that you get frameworks on which fingers to use in different situations.
So by studying scales and applying what you learn to other exercises and songs, you will know which fingers you should be using.
What we have discussed about what fingers to use also applies to pick directions.
For the same reasons that you should be using the same fingers every time,
you should be using the same pick direction every time.
If the piece of music you're working on does not have fingers and pick directions marked on it,
and you're struggling to remember which fingers and pick directions to use,
mark them on your music.
Reflection
A key part of your practice time is the few minutes after your practice.
When you finish a practice session, take a minute to reflect on how the practice session went.
Is there anything you can improve about how you approached your practice that you can change tomorrow?
Did any problems come up with what you were practicing that you need to fix next time you practice?
Take a minute to make a note of these thoughts and refer back to them the following day before you practice.
You could keep a specific practice log or just make some notes in your day planner.
The key thing is a simple system that is easy for you to use.
Take your time. Everyone is in such a rush. Take your time.
I know that you want to be a better guitar player and that you want to get there as quickly as possible.
Who doesn't? But when it comes to working on an exercise, you have to be patient.
Often, guitar players will play an exercise once and move on.
When you play that exercise, how do you know that you didn't get lucky with that playthrough?
You want to make sure that you can play an exercise correctly at least twice,
ideally three times in a row before you move on to something new.
I have a nice anecdote about this.
When I was in music college, I learned a cool, sweet-picking lick.
I went to a rehearsal and showed my friend.
He then asked me to play it a second time, and a big string of garbage came out of my guitar.
What I had learned was cool, but I wasn't yet able to use it in musical situations as part of my guitar playing.
He told me, if you can't play it twice, you can't play it, and that stuck with me.
That was also the last time I made that practice mistake.
If you are practicing something that requires a deep focus on muscle memory,
then you may want to continue practicing an exercise that you can do for a week before increasing the tempo, moving on to something new.
This goes back to the levels of learning we covered earlier, with conscious subconscious levels.
Once you have got something, you are using your conscious mind to play the technique.
However, we want these techniques to be part of our subconscious mind.
Repeatedly, practicing a conscious level technique will, over time, push that technique down into your subconscious.
Muscle tension
When you are a beginner, you will find learning guitar uncomfortable.
Short of ballet dancing, learning guitar is probably one of the most uncomfortable things you can do with your body.
You have to position yourself in a very unsymmetrical position and focus on very fine motor skills.
When we are learning guitar, one element that we are learning is how to use certain muscle groups in certain ways,
which is something you can say of any skill.
You will find that you are unable to control your muscles in the way you want,
and you will almost certainly find that your muscles do odd things that you don't want them to do.
A lot of students find that when concentrating, they introduce additional muscle tension into their bodies.
A good example of this is shoulder tension.
When approaching a section of music a student knows they struggle with,
they will tense their shoulders and hunch their back over the guitar,
sometimes so much so that it is obvious to anyone watching.
Next time you're practicing a piece of music that is difficult,
stop and ask yourself if you're feeling tenser than you need to be.
Another way muscle tension is introduced is just because,
which is where you needlessly tense up anytime you're playing the guitar.
This could be any muscle group from your feet and legs to your tongue.
Again, next time you sit down with your guitar,
ask yourself if you are needlessly tensing up muscle groups that do not need to be tense.
How much

How much muscle tension should you use? Just enough and no more. You need to use enough tension to ensure the notes ring out correctly and no more than that. Additional tension is not only wasted energy but something that will inhibit your playing.
Sympathetic muscle tension
This is when a muscle group tenses in reaction to a different muscle group being used.
For example, let's say you are tremolo picking a series of notes.
Your pick hand will tense up, which is necessary to perform the technique correctly,
but often students find that their fret hand will also tense up.
Now, the fretting hand does not need to hold down the strings any harder than normal for the picking hand to play them,
so this additional muscle tension is completely unnecessary.
If you find yourself doing this, you will want to train yourself to stop doing it.
Take your guitar and play a single note repeatedly.
Vary the tension in your pick hand while trying to keep your fret hand at the same consistent level of tension.
This will take a bit of trial and error to get right,
but you will find that after a bit of practice, maybe 5 to 10 minutes a day,
your body starts to figure it out and you will relax a bit more when playing.
Reduce muscle tension with good posture. A lot of muscle tension problems can be solved by
improving your posture. There is an appendix at the end with plenty of photographs to demonstrate
good posture. Dealing with frustration. When working on a difficult piece of music that is
slightly beyond your ability, it is natural to become frustrated with it. When this happens,
it is important to relax before continuing. Take a three-minute break, make a cup of tea,
and go outside for a few minutes. When frustrated, we often start to tense up our body,
which will make the piece that we are working on even harder to play.

paragraphs.en: If the piece of music you're working on does not have fingers and pick directions marked on it, and you're struggling to remember which fingers and pick directions to use, mark them on your music.
paragraphs.ca: Si el fragment de música que treballes no té els dits ni les direccions de pua indicats i et costa recordar quins dits i quines direccions de pua fer servir, marca'ls a la partitura.

paragraphs.en: Reflection
paragraphs.ca: Reflexió

paragraphs.en: A key part of your practice time is the few minutes after your practice. When you finish a practice session, take a minute to reflect on how the practice session went.
paragraphs.ca: Una part clau del temps de pràctica són els pocs minuts posteriors a la pràctica. Quan acabis una sessió de pràctica, dedica un minut a reflexionar sobre com ha anat.

paragraphs.en: Is there anything you can improve about how you approached your practice that you can change tomorrow? Did any problems come up with what you were practicing that you need to fix next time you practice?
paragraphs.ca: Hi ha res que puguis millorar en la manera com has enfocat la pràctica i que puguis canviar demà? Ha sorgit algun problema amb allò que practicaves que hagis de resoldre la propera vegada que practiquis?

paragraphs.en: Take a minute to make a note of these thoughts and refer back to them the following day before you practice. You could keep a specific practice log or just make some notes in your day planner.
paragraphs.ca: Dedica un minut a apuntar aquests pensaments i torna-los a llegir l'endemà abans de practicar. Pots portar un registre de pràctica específic o simplement fer unes notes a la teva agenda.

paragraphs.en: The key thing is a simple system that is easy for you to use.
paragraphs.ca: La clau és un sistema senzill i fàcil de fer servir per a tu.

paragraphs.en: Take your time. Everyone is in such a rush. Take your time. I know that you want to be a better guitar player and that you want to get there as quickly as possible.
paragraphs.ca: Pren-t'ho amb calma. Tothom va amb tanta pressa. Pren-t'ho amb calma. Sé que vols ser un guitarrista millor i que vols arribar-hi tan de pressa com sigui possible.

paragraphs.en: Who doesn't? But when it comes to working on an exercise, you have to be patient. Often, guitar players will play an exercise once and move on.
paragraphs.ca: Qui no ho vol? Però quan es tracta de treballar un exercici, has de tenir paciència. Sovint els guitarristes toquen un exercici una vegada i passen a una altra cosa.

paragraphs.en: When you play that exercise, how do you know that you didn't get lucky with that playthrough? You want to make sure that you can play an exercise correctly at least twice, ideally three times in a row before you move on to something new.
paragraphs.ca: Quan toques aquell exercici, com saps que no has tingut sort en aquella passada? Vols assegurar-te que pots tocar un exercici correctament com a mínim dues vegades, idealment tres seguides, abans de passar a una cosa nova.

paragraphs.en: I have a nice anecdote about this. When I was in music college, I learned a cool, sweet-picking lick. I went to a rehearsal and showed my friend.
paragraphs.ca: Tinc una bona anècdota sobre això. Quan estudiava al conservatori, vaig aprendre un lick ben bonic de sweep picking. Vaig anar a un assaig i el vaig ensenyar a un amic.

paragraphs.en: He then asked me to play it a second time, and a big string of garbage came out of my guitar. What I had learned was cool, but I wasn't yet able to use it in musical situations as part of my guitar playing.
paragraphs.ca: Llavors em va demanar que el toqués una segona vegada, i de la meva guitarra en va sortir una bona colla de porqueria. El que havia après era bonic, però encara no era capaç de fer-lo servir en situacions musicals dins del meu joc a la guitarra.

paragraphs.en: He told me, if you can't play it twice, you can't play it, and that stuck with me. That was also the last time I made that practice mistake.
paragraphs.ca: Em va dir: si no el pots tocar dues vegades, no el saps tocar. I això se'm va quedar gravat. També va ser l'última vegada que vaig cometre aquell error de pràctica.

paragraphs.en: If you are practicing something that requires a deep focus on muscle memory, then you may want to continue practicing an exercise that you can do for a week before increasing the tempo, moving on to something new.
paragraphs.ca: Si estàs practicant una cosa que requereix una concentració profunda en la memòria muscular, potser voldràs seguir practicant un exercici que ja domines durant una setmana abans d'augmentar el tempo o de passar a una cosa nova.

paragraphs.en: This goes back to the levels of learning we covered earlier, with conscious subconscious levels. Once you have got something, you are using your conscious mind to play the technique.
paragraphs.ca: Això ens remet als nivells d'aprenentatge que hem vist abans, amb els nivells conscient i subconscient. Quan tot just domines una cosa, fas servir la ment conscient per tocar la tècnica.

paragraphs.en: However, we want these techniques to be part of our subconscious mind. Repeatedly, practicing a conscious level technique will, over time, push that technique down into your subconscious.
paragraphs.ca: En canvi, volem que aquestes tècniques formin part de la nostra ment subconscient. Practicar repetidament una tècnica de nivell conscient l'empenyerà, amb el temps, cap al subconscient.

paragraphs.en: Muscle tension When you are a beginner, you will find learning guitar uncomfortable. Short of ballet dancing, learning guitar is probably one of the most uncomfortable things you can do with your body.
paragraphs.ca: Tensió muscular. Quan ets principiant, aprendre guitarra et resultarà incòmode. Tret del ballet, aprendre guitarra és probablement una de les coses més incòmodes que pots fer amb el cos.

paragraphs.en: You have to position yourself in a very unsymmetrical position and focus on very fine motor skills. When we are learning guitar, one element that we are learning is how to use certain muscle groups in certain ways, which is something you can say of any skill.
paragraphs.ca: Has de posar-te en una posició molt asimètrica i concentrar-te en habilitats motrius molt fines. Quan aprenem guitarra, un dels elements que aprenem és com fer servir certs grups musculars de certes maneres, cosa que es pot dir de qualsevol habilitat.

paragraphs.en: You will find that you are unable to control your muscles in the way you want, and you will almost certainly find that your muscles do odd things that you don't want them to do.
paragraphs.ca: Veuràs que no ets capaç de controlar els músculs com voldries i, gairebé segur, que els teus músculs fan coses estranyes que no vols que facin.

paragraphs.en: A lot of students find that when concentrating, they introduce additional muscle tension into their bodies. A good example of this is shoulder tension.
paragraphs.ca: A molts alumnes els passa que, quan es concentren, introdueixen tensió muscular addicional al cos. Un bon exemple és la tensió a les espatlles.

paragraphs.en: When approaching a section of music a student knows they struggle with, they will tense their shoulders and hunch their back over the guitar, sometimes so much so that it is obvious to anyone watching.
paragraphs.ca: Quan s'afronta un passatge de música que l'alumne sap que li costa, tensa les espatlles i encorba l'esquena sobre la guitarra, de vegades tant que és evident per a qualsevol que ho vegi.

paragraphs.en: Next time you're practicing a piece of music that is difficult, stop and ask yourself if you're feeling tenser than you need to be.
paragraphs.ca: La propera vegada que practiquis un fragment de música difícil, atura't i pregunta't si estàs més tens del que caldria.

paragraphs.en: Another way muscle tension is introduced is just because, which is where you needlessly tense up anytime you're playing the guitar.
paragraphs.ca: Una altra manera d'introduir tensió muscular és simplement perquè sí, és a dir, tensar-te innecessàriament sempre que toques la guitarra.

paragraphs.en: This could be any muscle group from your feet and legs to your tongue. Again, next time you sit down with your guitar, ask yourself if you are needlessly tensing up muscle groups that do not need to be tense.
paragraphs.ca: Pot ser qualsevol grup muscular, des dels peus i les cames fins a la llengua. Un altre cop, la propera vegada que seguis amb la guitarra, pregunta't si estàs tensant innecessàriament grups musculars que no caldria que estiguessin tensos.

paragraphs.en: How much How much muscle tension should you use? Just enough and no more. You need to use enough tension to ensure the notes ring out correctly and no more than that. Additional tension is not only wasted energy but something that will inhibit your playing.
paragraphs.ca: Quanta tensió muscular. Quanta tensió muscular hauries de fer servir? La justa, i no més. Has de fer servir prou tensió perquè les notes sonin correctament i no més que això. La tensió addicional no només és energia malgastada, sinó que també perjudicarà el teu joc.

paragraphs.en: Sympathetic muscle tension This is when a muscle group tenses in reaction to a different muscle group being used. For example, let's say you are tremolo picking a series of notes.
paragraphs.ca: Tensió muscular simpàtica. Es produeix quan un grup muscular es tensa com a reacció a l'ús d'un altre grup muscular. Per exemple, diguem que estàs fent pua tremolada en una sèrie de notes.

paragraphs.en: Your pick hand will tense up, which is necessary to perform the technique correctly, but often students find that their fret hand will also tense up.
paragraphs.ca: La mà de la pua es tensarà, cosa necessària per executar la tècnica correctament, però sovint els alumnes veuen que la mà dels trastes també se'ls tensa.

paragraphs.en: Now, the fretting hand does not need to hold down the strings any harder than normal for the picking hand to play them, so this additional muscle tension is completely unnecessary.
paragraphs.ca: Ara bé, la mà dels trastes no necessita prémer les cordes més fort del normal perquè la mà de la pua les pugui tocar, així que aquesta tensió muscular addicional és completament innecessària.

paragraphs.en: If you find yourself doing this, you will want to train yourself to stop doing it. Take your guitar and play a single note repeatedly.
paragraphs.ca: Si veus que fas això, voldràs entrenar-te per deixar de fer-ho. Agafa la guitarra i toca una sola nota repetidament.

paragraphs.en: Vary the tension in your pick hand while trying to keep your fret hand at the same consistent level of tension. This will take a bit of trial and error to get right, but you will find that after a bit of practice, maybe 5 to 10 minutes a day, your body starts to figure it out and you will relax a bit more when playing.
paragraphs.ca: Varia la tensió de la mà de la pua mentre intentes mantenir la mà dels trastes amb un nivell de tensió constant. Caldrà una mica de prova i error per encertar-ho, però veuràs que, després d'una mica de pràctica, potser 5 o 10 minuts al dia, el teu cos comença a entendre-ho i et relaxaràs una mica més quan toquis.

paragraphs.en: Reduce muscle tension with good posture. A lot of muscle tension problems can be solved by improving your posture. There is an appendix at the end with plenty of photographs to demonstrate good posture. Dealing with frustration. When working on a difficult piece of music that is slightly beyond your ability, it is natural to become frustrated with it. When this happens, it is important to relax before continuing. Take a three-minute break, make a cup of tea,
paragraphs.ca: Reduir la tensió muscular amb una bona postura. Molts problemes de tensió muscular es poden resoldre millorant la postura. Al final hi ha un apèndix amb moltes fotografies que mostren una bona postura. Com gestionar la frustració. Quan treballes un fragment de música difícil que està una mica per sobre de les teves capacitats, és natural frustrar-te'n. Quan passi això, és important relaxar-se abans de continuar. Fes una pausa de tres minuts, prepara't una tassa de te

paragraphs.en: and go outside for a few minutes. When frustrated, we often start to tense up our body, which will make the piece that we are working on even harder to play.
paragraphs.ca: i surt a fora uns minuts. Quan estem frustrats, sovint comencem a tensar el cos, cosa que fa que el fragment que estem treballant encara sigui més difícil de tocar.

segments.text: The myth of perfection. Perfection is a goal that we will never reach. This isn't to say we
shouldn't aim for it, but if we use it as a goal, we will never be happy or learn anything new.
It can be tempting to say that you will only move on to the next exercise once you have the current
exercise perfect, but this is a trap. Your current exercise will never be perfect. You will never
move to the next exercise and you will never progress. Instead, aim to get what you're working
on 80% to 90% correct, and then move on to the next exercise. You will often find that by doing
this, when you revisit an earlier exercise, that last 10 to 20% has magically developed.
The reason for doing this is that when we aim for perfection, the 80-20 rule starts to work
against us. The 80-20 rule states that it takes 20% of the effort to get 80% of the results,
Or to put it another way, 80% of the effort only generates 20% of the results.
Getting 80% of the results and moving on is a much more effective way to progress quickly
than spending all your time getting the last little bit right.
The exception to this is if you are practicing for a performance or recording session.
In that case, you would want to make sure you have all the little detail worked out,
which will take enormous amounts of time,
so make sure you plan for the extra time that you will need.
Problem-solving strategies.
When practicing, you're going to come across sections of music and exercises that you struggle with,
and it's important that you have a selection of tools to tackle those problems as they arise.
The general approach to solving any problem with your guitar playing is as follows.
1. Figure out exactly what the problem is.
2. Isolate the problem.
3. Practice that specific thing until you get it right.
4. Slowly reintegrate back into the piece.
Start at a slow tempo and work your way up.
When figuring out the problem, you have to be specific.
Really specific.
I can't play this is not specific.
I can't play the chord change is better.
I can't move from E minor to G is better.
When moving from E minor to G,
my first finger on my left hand goes to the wrong string is best.
This gives you the information you need to fix the problem.
You can now focus on moving that first finger correctly and fixing your problem.
So when you are trying to diagnose your guitar playing problems,
take a minute to think through what is going on and be as specific as possible.
Sometimes when playing, it can be difficult to figure out what our hands are doing
as we are so focused on playing.
If this is the case, video yourself on your phone and watch the video back and figure out what it is you are doing.
Next, we'll look at some specific strategies that you can use to fix the problems that you are having.
Isolation
Let's say you are working on a song that is five minutes long.
Most guitar players tend to practice songs by playing through them from start to finish.
Let's also say that there is a chord change you are struggling with towards the end of the song.
A lot of players will practice by playing through the song,
hitting the difficult chord change,
screwing up and going back to the start for a second attempt.
Earlier in the book, we talked about the distinction between practicing and playing.
In this case, you are spending most of your practice time playing the guitar and not practicing.
95% of the song is within your ability.
It is only the 5%, that chord change at the end, that needs to be practiced.
So why not spend all the practice time practicing the hard stuff?
A more efficient way to practice would be to take the chord change at the end
and set up a loop using Guitar Pro, or your DAW,
to practice that specific part of the song that you are struggling with.
Let's also say that you have 30 minutes to practice a day.
In 30 minutes, the 5-minute song can be played 6 times.
That's not very many times.
It's going to take a while to get that last chord change correct
if you can only play it 6 times.
The problematic chord change is in a 15-second section of music.
If you were to isolate and practice the difficult chord change,
you could practice that 120 times in 30 minutes.
120 repetitions versus 6 repetitions.
So in this example, by practicing using isolation,
you will progress 120 times faster than if you play the song all the way through from start to finish.
This isn't to say that you should never play songs from start to finish.
You should, and doing so is important to practice, especially if you are rehearsing for a gig.
But when there is something you are struggling with, isolate it and work intensely on it to solve it.
Then go back to playing the song all the way through.
Isolation to the ridiculous.
When practicing, you may find that your hands do weird things from time to time.
When you find this happening, you can take the concept of isolation to the extreme
and isolate the specific hand that is causing the problem.
For example, if your left hand is doing something weird,
take the motion that you are trying to achieve and practice moving your left hand that way.
Don't worry about the right hand.
Put it down by your side so that it doesn't distract you.
Just focus on moving your left hand correctly.
You will find that after 5 to 10 minutes, you have solved the problem.
If you have a problem with your right hand, for example, trying a complex string skipping pattern,
then you can do exactly the same thing. Put your left hand down by your side and practice moving
the right hand correctly, just playing through open strings. You can take this even further
and apply it to individual finer movements that are proving problematic.
Synchronization. This technique applies specifically to scale-based problems you may
be having. When we start to push the limits of how fast we can play with scale-based exercises,
the two hands often start to go out of sync with each other.
We can improve that by playing each note in the exercise twice.
As an example, let's say you were working on the following melody.
Figure 8, tab example.
When we double up each note, we get figure 9, tab example.
Note that we are keeping the same note value as the original.
In this case, everything is being played with 8th notes.
We would be using alternate picking in this case.
By playing the exercise like this, we force our hands to move at different rates.
In the original exercise, we pick eighth notes, and our fret hand also changes with eighth notes.
In the second exercise, our pick hand is still playing eighth notes, but now the fretting hand is moving at a quarter note speed.
You will find playing the exercise this way does wonders for your synchronization,
and will help you push the original exercise to higher tempos while being more accurate.
Practicing chord changes.
I thought I would add this section as something a lot of guitar players struggle with
is improving their chord changes.
They either can't change fast enough,
or their fingers can't find the right place on the neck,
or their fingers just do weird stuff.
So here are some of my best tips for improving your chord changes on guitar.
Grip and release.
This is a simple and highly effective exercise.
Hold the cord down really, really hard.
You should be holding it down so hard that the tips of your fingernails turn yellow.
Hold the cord down like this for 6 to 8 seconds, then relax.
When you relax, completely relax your arm and hand down by your side.
When telling students to relax their arm completely,
I often see them relax their hand partially, which is not what I ask them to do.
So make sure that you relax your arm completely. You must relax your arm as you are introducing
massive amounts of tension into your arm and that needs to be dissipated. Repeat the exercise
five to six times for each chord that you are working on. You will find that this exercise
helps your fingers find the chord faster. Slow changes. When it comes to moving your hand to a
new chord, there are two stages. One, moving the hand so that the hand is roughly over the correct
frets. Two, move your fingers to the right strings and frets. Step one is quite easy. Moving your arm
horizontally up or down a few frets on the guitar doesn't take any skill or thought. Step two is a
lot trickier. You have to use precise motor skills to hold down the correct chord. Your ability to
execute step one quickly will often far exceed your ability to execute step two quickly. Often,
a student will move their hand quickly to the right position, then their fingers will flail
around as they try to hold down the cord as quickly as they move their hand, which they
cannot do. I like to call this effect Bambi on ice, as their fingers look like a baby deer trying
to stand whilst walking on ice. But in all seriousness, this creates a problem. Every time
you move your hand this way, you are practicing wiggling your fingers. You are not practicing
holding down the cord correctly. You need to practice moving your fingers directly to where
they need to go, not going all over the neck before they find the right spot. To fix this,
take your hand off the guitar, relax it by your side, then bring your hand back to the neck,
slowly. Make sure each finger moves directly to where it needs to go to hold down the chord that
you are learning. You should not be rearranging your fingers, and they should not be wiggling or
dancing over the strings. If they do any of these things, you are moving too fast, and you must
slow down. You may be surprised at just how slowly you need to move your fingers to do this correctly,
but take the time. The secret to learning guitar quickly is to practice things slowly.
Practicing too fast is not practicing at all, it's just wasting time. You can also apply this
exercise to moving between two chords. Right hand always in time. We often struggle when
practicing a new chord change because it's new. This is normal and to be expected. So when
practicing, we'll be playing through a few chords, we get to the one that we are struggling with,
and we can't quite play it in time. Every time we get to that chord, it takes us a little longer
to find it than the other chords that we are playing. We move our fret hand to the correct
position, it takes us a little longer to find that position, and then our strumming hand finally
strums the strings, much later than we wanted to. Every time we do this, we are practicing
playing out of time. We are practicing leaving extra time for this particular chord. Here's
how we fix that. Play through the chord progression using a metronome and keep the strumming hand
perfectly in time, even if the left hand can't find the chord. This will be quite difficult,
as you've been practicing playing the chord out of time for so long. And when you do this,
you will find that you make a horrible sound from your guitar. And when you do it the next time,
you will find that you still make a horrible sound from your guitar. But if you persist,
you will find that after 10 to 15 repetitions, your chord change starts to feel a bit smoother.
If it doesn't start feeling better after 10 to 15 repetitions, then slow down the metronome
and isolate the chord change. See the previous section on isolation.
This is a weird way to practice, but it is very effective.
Think ahead.
When you start to become a bit more advanced at guitar,
you have to start moving your body and thinking out of time with the music
to be able to play in time.
This is a good example of that idea.
When you are holding down a particular chord,
you are holding down that particular chord.
Obvious, right?
This means that you do not need to be thinking about that chord.
This means that you can be thinking about the next chord that you want to play.
While holding down any particular chord, have your brain think ahead about what the next chord will be.
Try and visualize it in your mind and you will find your fingers can find it a little easier.
