segments.text: Appendix 1. Sample Libraries. Sound Libraries.
These are a great way to get more realism in your demos and can also be used in final releases.
Some people like to compose directly with sound libraries.
Sound libraries are pre-recorded instruments.
For example, someone will record all the notes that a violin can play,
then you program your DW via MIDI,
and it plays back the notes you programmed using the pre-recorded violin.
Libraries can take up huge amounts of space,
not only for storage, but in your RAM.
You will probably need an external hard drive to store the libraries you use,
and you may need to upgrade your RAM.
Some libraries include a player.
This is the software that stitches together sound samples based on the parts you have written.
Some libraries do not include the player and adjust samples.
These libraries require a third-party player to work.
The most common third-party player is Contact.
Link 1. Orchestral sample libraries.
Orchestral libraries require some knowledge of MIDI programming to get the most out of them.
You will have to learn how to program velocity and a couple of MIDI CC channels to get them working as well as possible.
I would advise watching reviews of libraries on YouTube, reading the manual for libraries you get,
and you may even consider finding someone to give a few lessons on how to program effectively.
Big Cat
If you want a free library, there is a guy called Big Cat who has done a vocal library here, Link2.
There is also an orchestral library here, Link 4, both of which can be downloaded for free.
EastWest Composer Cloud.
This is a $20 per month subscription that gives you access to nearly the entire EW library.
This is what I use, Link 3.
It is one of the best libraries available.
EastWest Symphonic Orchestra.
EastWest Symphonic Orchestra is $400, and while that is a big chunk of change,
it's at the lower end of the price spectrum for tools like this.
From a dollars for sound quality perspective,
it's probably the best priced option.
This library is included in EW Composer Cloud.
Spitfire BBC Orchestra.
Spitfire offers a limited version of one of their libraries for £49.
Link 5.
I have mixed feelings about this.
Great price point and a limited choice of articulations.
But if all you want is some nice sustained strings and a few horns here and there, it could work for you.
You can also apply to them to get it for free. I think one of my students did this.
Other libraries.
The other big libraries are Vienna Symphonic Library,
https colon slash slash www.vsl.co.at slash en,
orchestral tools, link 6, and sign samples, link 7,
all of which are quite pricey,
but these are things composers use in movies and TV shows.
These are top-level pro libraries, StaffPad libraries.
If you're going to use StaffPad for composing,
it has libraries broken into orchestral sections, strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion,
and priced at $80 each, roughly. They also have pianos, harps, harpsichords, church organs,
and a few other instruments, including guitar. Other things. Some libraries require the contact
player from native instruments, Link 8. The player comes with, I think, some orchestral samples,
but I don't know how they stand up against the other big names.
One of the nice things about East-West libraries is that they have their own player.
Rock and drum sample libraries tend to be a bit more out-of-the-box than orchestral tools,
as the dynamics involved are not as complex, but most will still benefit from some programming.
When it comes to rock, pop and metal, a company called Toontrack is the dominating company,
the industry. Link 9. Logic Pro Drummer. It's worth noting that Logic Pro comes with a pretty
good built-in drum sample library. Their drummer tool can automatically create drum beats for you.
You can drag the drummer file to a different MIDI track and have a different library playback the
drums part Logic created. Most doors come with semi-decent built-in drum samples.
East West Ministry of Rock
This has a collection of drums, bass guitars and guitars.
This is a nice all-rounder to give your demos some more realism.
It's included in East West Composer Cloud.
Link 10
I've used the bass guitars a lot when creating demos and backing tracks for myself.
TuneTrack EZ Drummer
This is a great go-to drum library.
It's hard to go wrong with this.
Link 11
TuneTrack Superior Drummer
This is the big brother to EZ Drummer, giving incredible sound control and programming options.
Link 12
Superior Drummer is more than a sample library.
It is a full drum production door in a plug-in that can also be run independently to your door.
Get Good Drums
This is the brainchild of Nolly and Matt from the band Periphery.
Their libraries are quite cheap as they use Contact Player.
They also offer some presets for a Kemper.
Link 13. Appendix 2. Books worth studying. Writing better lyrics. Pat Patterson. This is a great
introduction to lyric writing, going in-depth into several techniques and approaches with
exercises to get your lyric writing skills up to scratch. Orchestration. Walter Piston. This book
is a classic, giving a comprehensive overview of the instruments in an orchestra and also
different musical textures that can be created with those instruments.
Harmony, Walter Piston. A good, although sometimes complex, overview of common practice period
harmony and how it works. A great introduction to composing more in-depth with the CPP approach.
Guitar Secrets, Joe Satriani. This is a collection of articles that Joe Satriani wrote for a guitar
magazine way back. It's a great insight into his mind with good exercises to work on.
Rock Discipline, John Petrucci. This is a legendary book with exercises to work on developing your rock guitar technique.
Counterpoint, Alfred Mann, J. Fuchs. This book is a foundation of Western music theory practice and was studied by Beethoven and Mozart.
The book has a unique approach, written in the style of a lecture from a master to a student, written by J. Fuchs and translated by Alfred Mann.
Some things are poorly explained, or not explained at all,
but it is a good starting point for anyone with a serious interest in music theory.
A.B. Guide to Music Theory, Volume 1, Eric Taylor
This book is a fantastic introduction to music theory,
and I would strongly recommend it to everyone getting started with music theory.
It is probably the best introduction to music theory I've seen.
Introduction to Tonal Theory, Peter Westergaard
This is probably the densest and most in-depth book on the technical aspects of composition I have ever read.
I'm still only 25% through the book.
It's out of print and quite expensive to find a copy.
If you want a serious deep dive into tonal music, this is one of the greatest books on the subject.

segments.text: Appendix 6. Useful software.
This is a list of programs that I have found useful over the years.
Guitar Pro.
This is the best guitar tablature writing program available.
It prioritizes tab entry over notation entry, but is capable of both.
You can create beautiful and clear tabs and parts for all instruments and play them back.
You can add scale, arpeggio, and chord diagrams to your tabs.
Playback sounds aren't great.
I usually use the clean sound for all guitar parts because it sounds nicer than the distortion sound.
Orchestral instruments can sound pretty bad.
Musescore.
This is a free program.
Musescore is mainly designed for orchestral instruments but can handle guitar tabs.
Working in guitar tab does take some setting up, not much, which is not intuitive,
but there are tutorials on how to do this.
MuseScore does not have as many tab features as Guitar Pro, but it has enough to make a good tab.
It has a nice feature where you can drag notes between strings, which makes rearranging parts for the guitar very fast.
MuseScore has good tab entry and great notation entry features.
Using MuseScore is a bit more complex than Guitar Pro.
MuseScore also has a nice feature where you can break a score up,
inserting text boxes between sections of music.
This is great for teachers who want to create worksheets for students.
The default orchestral sounds are much better than Guitar Pro.
Logic Pro X LPX. This is a DAW.
LPX is great for recording music.
You can also create quite nice-looking scores and guitar tabs.
